📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it is a truth universally acknowledged that a single TV in need of decent sound must be in want of one of the best soundbars. And, likely, you're here because you're sick of awful-sounding TV speakers — well, I've got the list for you. We've spent a lot of time testing the best soundbars to make sure you get the best bang for your buck.

Sources indicate that the best is still the Sonos Arc Ultra. It's an absolute stunner of a soundbar, bringing great sound, lovely Dolby Atmos, and even slick styling so you won't mind it sitting under your TV. It does come with a substantial wallet-denting price, though — if you're looking to save some money, we'd go for the also excellent Sony HT-S100F.

But each soundbar we've listed here would make a great addition to your TV setup, so whether you're shopping on a budget, need something to work with your existing tech or just need a few more options to choose from, these are the best soundbars we've tested that I recommend right now.

The Tom's Guide testing team is an experienced bunch who love good sound. Here's why you can trust us to find the best soundbar for your needs:.

From the time I built a surround system from the cheapest stuff I could find on eBay to reviewing the latest and greatest sound gear, I put a whole lot of time and effort into working out which soundbars are worth your money. I've constructed this guide with input from the rest of the team so that we can use our experience to guide you through your soundbar journey.

Recent findings suggest that when I’m testing soundbars, I put them through their paces in our state-of-the-art testing suite, complete with a top-of-the-range Panasonic OLED TV and an array of 4K Ultra HD Blu-Rays. I’m looking for soundbars that make movies come to life — both budget-friendly and premium.

Sources indicate that as a reviews writer, I put soundbars through rigorous testing by analyzing sound quality across various film and TV genres, connectivity options, and determine whether they're the best value for money. I love watching movies at the theater, so I like a soundbar that can closely replicate the sound via Dolby Atmos. I also play a lot of video games on my PS5 and there's nothing better than a soundbar that makes you feel like you're actually a sword-wielding samurai in feudal Japan.

Before we dive deep into the best soundbars, I just want to go through what we look for when we're testing them. We make sure to evaluate the soundbar in some key areas.

Setup: While it's something you're only going to do once, we want to make sure that it's as easy as possible to get working. Plug-and-play is the name of the game here, and if there are extra features we want to make sure that they're as easy as possible to use.

According to recent reports, how big is it? Everyone's space is different. Maybe you've got a massive room with loads of stuff in it, or maybe your living room is more compact and minimal. You want a soundbar that's going to suit your space, and, more importantly, not going to take up too much of it. We check whether the soundbar fits under our 50-inch OLED Philips testing TV to make sure you're not going to have any size concerns. Ultimately, it needs to fit on your TV stand.

Are there any extras? What's in the box, and are its contents any good? Some soundbars come with extras like surround speakers and subwoofers. I want to make sure that those extras are worth it, and that they're not just pictures to sell them at the store.

Sources indicate that sound: This is arguably the most key part of the soundbar, and there are a number of things we look out for here. How's the dialog? Is it clear, or muffled? What about the bass — are you going to have rumbling floors in your movies, or are there going to be problems with the low end? I love testing the sound portion because I get to watch movies instead of working; But it's still important when testing and working out whether a bar is for you.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Sonos Arc Ultra is the best soundbar around. It's not cheap, but it's surround sound and Dolby Atmos performance beats just about anything else that lacks separate surround speakers. I'll almost certainly never watch movies with anything else for some time.

According to recent reports, the Sonos Arc Ultra is more than just a soundbar. It's a fully fledged audio entertainment center that connects to your TV and just happens to be really good for movies and TV.

I particularly like how you can stream your music to it from any device — I frequently find myself spending a bunch of time listening to my favorite tunes from Qobuz and Tidal with it, thanks to its ease of use.

In a recent development, but it's really that epic movie experience you're looking for with something like the Sonos Arc Ultra, and you get it in spades. The Dolby Atmos with just the soundbar is unlike anything else around, and if you add in the optional surrounds, it's a game-changer.

I absolutely love watching just about anything with the Arc Ultra — although you will want to pick up a Sonos sub so that you can get the low-end grunt your movies deserve. It's not cheap — but it is so, so worth it.

Recent findings suggest that setupSetting up your Arc Ultra is going to take a bit more effort than some of the other options on the list. I found it fairly easy though, given the excellent instructions. If all you want to do is use the soundbar, you just plug it into power, plug the HDMI port into the back of the soundbar and the HDMI ARC port of your TV, and it should work without problems at all. I did have to change the settings in my Samsung TV sound menu to make sure that the device was set as the primary sound output, but then it worked with no problem.

If you want to use the excellent Sonos room correction settings, smart features, or to connect other Sonos speakers as surrounds, things will get more complicated. You'll need to use the Sonos App for these — and while it's not difficult, it is extra work. The room correction options also need you to move around the room while waving your phone around, so if mobility is something you struggle with, you may want to look elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that once set up, you won't have any concerns, but it's worth bearing in mind that it takes more work to get it working. It's all absolutely worth your time though, with massive boosts to sound quality and useful features within the Sonos App.

How big is itThe Sonos Arc Ultra is a big soundbar. It's very long, measuring around four feet long. I found it perfectly suited for TVs larger than 55 inches, although if your TV is smaller, things might look out of place.

There's less of a problem with the height. It's only about 3 inches tall, so it'll fit under most TVs without a problem.

According to recent reports, are there any extrasYou get the soundbar in a box — there's no included subwoofer here. Not that you really need one, though, given that Sonos has managed to pack some incredible bassy hardware into its slim frame.

If you want to enhance your movie-watching experience, though, you can add in a Sonos sub and surrounds in the form of Era 100 or Era 300 speakers. It adds to the cost, but it gets very close to dedicated home cinema sound.

SoundThis is the best bit of the Arc Ultra. I love the way that soundbar sounds for movies and TV, with some incredible body to the sound. I found the dialogue clear while watching the news and other TV demonstrates, and it was excellent when listening to Sir David Attenborough talk to me about dinosaurs in Prehistoric Planet.

For movies, as you might expect, the Arc Ultra dominates. I discovered that even without extra surrounds, the Dolby Atmos was amazing, putting me in the center of a space battle in Star Wars Episode 3. The bass without a sub is surprisingly good as well, although if you really want to feel your movies you should buy the extra subwoofer.

It has been revealed that it's pretty good for music as well, uncommon for a soundbar. There's plenty of space, thanks to the wider form factor, and the bar manages the low end of your tracks pretty well, too.

The Sony HT-S100F (HT-S150 in the U.K.) is a great-sounding soundbar for an epic price. It won't break the bank, but it'll increase the sound quality of your movies and TV far and above the sound from your TV speakers.

When you don't want to spend loads of money on a soundbar, something like the Sony HT-S100F is just what the doctor ordered. It's a lovely, cheap soundbar that does everything you need it to — make your TV sound better than the built-in audio.

In a recent development, it brings more clarity to dialogue, most importantly. Everything from your favorite movies all the way to news bulletins and everything in between become much easier to make out, perfect if you're struggling to hear what people are trying to say.

It's relatively compact as well, so you'll have no problems fitting it on your TV bench beneath most sizes of screen. Our tester found it super easy to use, with very few (if any) connection problems that sometimes plague cheaper devices.

It's not going to be as impressive as some of the more expensive options on the list, but it more than makes up for it with excellent clarity for all your watching.

According to recent reports, setupGetting the HT-S100F up and running is about as easy as they come. Just plug the power in, connect the HDMI port to the HDMI ARC on your TV, and it'll turn on automatically whenever you turn on your TV.

Erin did find that you might have to occasionally turn the bar on with the remote control, but it didn't happen enough to be a massive problem.

Sources indicate that how major is itThe HT-S100F is designed for normal-sized televisions, and its compact frame will fit on most TV stands. It measures 35 inches long, so you'll be fine for TVs from 32 inches to 50.

Sources indicate that it might seem a little small for larger TVs, though, with the screen dwarfing the soundbar beneath. You'll also find some minor sound complications with larger sets, as the picture feels wider than the sound that's coming out.

Height-wise you'll be fine with a range of different TVs as well. The bar measures just 2.5 inches tall, so it won't cover the bottom of your screen. If it covers the IR receiver of your TV, there's an IR repeater built in so that your controller still works.

Erin found it fit well underneath our 50-inch testing TV, although if you've got a larger TV set, you might want something slightly larger in the long run.

Are there any extras?In the box of the HT-S100F, you get the soundbar — and nothing else. You can't buy an extra subwoofer or surround either, leaving you with no upgrades for the future.

According to recent reports, this makes it great for just a simple setup, and it keeps the cost down. There's a controller in the box as well, so you can connect Bluetooth devices and change sources without standing up.

SoundThe HT-100F isn't going to blow you away if you're a movie lover, but its solid, serviceable sound is a big step-up over your TV's built-in speakers. It makes dialog clearer, music sounds better, and sound effects are easier to hear.

For music, things weren't quite so impressive, but if you've got no other ways to listen to music in the living room, it will more than suffice. If you're looking for a cheap way to get much better sound out of your TV watching, then this is the way to go.

It has been revealed that sony's mid-range soundbar brings smarts and excellent sound to a more affordable price point. It connects to your Wi-Fi for wireless listening and includes a good subwoofer for some extra sonic grunt. It's excellent for dialogue too, with crystal-clear voice work for movies and TV highlights alike.

In a recent development, sony's line of soundbars can cost a lot of money — but it's the mid-range and cheap offerings that we recommend the most. This, the Theater Bar 7, is the mid-range bar, and it offers some great value for money.

For one, the 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos sound is very good. The included sub offers some extra low-end for those all-notable explosions in action movies, and the surround sound is immersive and well produced. The dialogue department is where the soundbar really shines. Speech is clear and easily discernible over whatever else is going on on-screen.

There are also some useful smart features built in. You can connect to your Wi-Fi to stream music to the bar, and adjust settings from the app on your phone. As long as you don't expect the best musical sound, of course — as with so many soundbars, this is not a musical powerhouse but a rectangular movie hero. And that's OK.

Those with bigger TVs might also struggle slightly with the size. It's quite a compact soundbar, and that can affect the perception of sound in space when the image above it is much larger. Thankfully, the solid surround sound does a good job of keeping the effect to a minimum.

It should be noted that the Theater Bar 7 is not a cheap soundbar, but it's a great way of getting immersive sound without spending thousands on one of the range-topping devices.

In a recent development, setupFor any normal movie or TV watching, setting up the bar is very easy. Plug it into the power, and then into the HDMI ARC port on your TV. Plug in the subwoofer and everything connects together with no hassle at all.

In a recent development, nor is connecting the bar to the internet. Download the app, and then follow the on-screen instructions to get everything working properly. We recommend you dip into the settings menu from there and turn the bass up, and raise the surround height to 10. That gave us the best sound, although your room might require some fine tweaking.

Recent findings suggest that how significant is itThis is a fairly compact soundbar, measuring 37.5 inches long. That means that it's going to be dwarfed by larger TVs, but those measuring around 55 inches or smaller are going to be fine. Our testing TV is 55 inches, for example, and everything was fine.

Industry observers note that the subwoofer is thin and compact too, so you don't need as much space as you might for some of the competition. It fits perfectly beside a TV unit without sticking out like a sore thumb.

Industry observers note that are there any extrasThere's one very major extra in the box beside the remote control — that lovely big subwoofer for the low stuff. There aren't any extra surround speakers though, because they're all built into the bar itself.

Features-wise, though, you've got the mobile app to go with Bluetooth and wired audio connections. You can stream music to the bar from around the house, should you want some music when you're not watching movies. You can also use the app to change key settings of the bar, like sound profiles and bass levels.

Industry observers note that soundSony's audio chops are well documented, and the Theater Bar 7 just continues the legacy. There's some lovely bass on offer here, with impact and depth whenever the action on screen gets thick and fast. We used the app to dial in the bass a bit, though; out of the box it was tuned a bit low. Your mileage may vary, of course.

The dialogue was what really impressed here, though. Speech was clear and bright no matter what was going on around it, be that a fighter plane screeching through the skies or a car chase in the Batmobile. That's not to say it's ever in your face. When the goings get calmer, the voices adjust to match. You'll never miss a word.

Not everything is rosy, as it generally isn't with most soundbars. Music playback is disappointing, with merely an "OK" in our review. It's not bad, but there's no drive to the music as you'll find with movies and TV highlights. A shame, but not unexpected.

If you want a true surround sound package in one unit, then the 1300XMK2 could be just what you've been looking for. Its extra speakers attach to the bar itself, and then you can move them into position when you want to watch a movie. It's not cheap, but it's a movie monster.

Sources indicate that there’s not really such a thing as a “bargain” when it comes to home surround sound. Instead, there’s value — and the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 brings the value unlike just about anything. Flexibility, a more affordable price than the key competition, and, of course, great sound.

Sources indicate that the two ends of the soundbar can be disconnected and placed around the room, powered by their own internal batteries. If you don’t have the space for a traditional setup, this is a great way to enjoy immersive Dolby Atmos sound without a more permanent (and expensive) solution.

It has been revealed that the soundbar itself is quite large, however. It’s very deep and rather long with its surrounds attached, so you’ll need a long TV stand and substantial TV to make sure it doesn’t look out of place. There’s a subwoofer in the box that you’ll need to find space for as well.

The sound is great. It’s immersive, directional, deep and clear. We loved it when watching a wide range of movies, from action to romance. There’s little this soundbar can’t do.

SetupFirst off, hit the gym before you place this soundbar anywhere. This is a 26-pound behemoth, so you might even want two people to lift it into place on your TV stand. There are some extra setup quirks as well, but they’re easily mitigated thanks to the good instructions and user-friendly design.

Once you’ve plugged the soundbar and subwoofer into the wall, you’ll hook the soundbar into the eARC port of your TV. The soundbar and sub should find each other automatically, but if not, use the connection button on the sub.

If you want to use the surrounds, pull them off the soundbar and place them around your room. Sound adjustment is done automatically. If you have any wireless connection challenges, re-attach them to the soundbar to reset everything.

Streaming and Wi-Fi are handled by JBL’s ONE app. It’s super easy; we had no problems at all getting everything connected and working.

How major is itThere’s no two ways around it — the 1300XMK2 is a very big soundbar. At 40 inches, the soundbar is wide, and that's without taking extra surrounds into account. It’s very deep too, so you’ll want to make sure that there’s enough space on your TV stand that way. If not, we’d recommend wall mounting the TV.

Industry observers note that this is a bar suited to much larger TVs, 65-inch at a minimum. Otherwise you’ll risk the bar looking too big, and your TV small.

In a recent development, thankfully, you won’t have to worry about how tall the bar is. It’s short enough that most TVs will amply clear the top, so you don’t have to worry about the soundbar blocking the view. Just bear in mind that you’ll also want space for the surround speakers behind your seating position — they’re not going to work if they’re in front of you.

Are there any extrasYou get everything you need in the box. There’s the bar itself, along with the surround speakers. Unlike other models, from the likes of Sonos, this is a significant bonus and means you don’t have to buy any further devices for some lovely Dolby Atmos sound.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also a subwoofer in the box, along with all the cables you’d ever need for just about any circumstance. There’s a controller in the box, although we found that the JBL ONE app was a perfectly serviceable way of controlling the sound — or your TV remote through the eARC port.

It has been revealed that soundWith 23 drivers powering 11.1.4 channels, you’d hope the 1300XMK2 sounded good. And, sure enough, the bar sounds excellent. Those extra surrounds make sure that the sound is immersive and massive, while the sub adds impressive depth and bass.

The planes flying in Top Gun: Maverick made the room shake, and the soundtrack was bombastic during testing. The whole movie placed our tester directly in the movie.

Object placement is good too, making sure that everything is kept in the right place.

The soundbar was pretty good for music too, making soundtracks sound great, although it struggled slightly more with stereo tracks — but it's still better than most soundbars.

Recent findings suggest that want everything in one box but don't want to spend every single dollar you have? The QS750F is a great option, with extra surround speakers and a subwoofer for less than $1000.

Industry observers note that soundbars are expensive — there’s no way around that. You want to achieve the best bang-for-buck sound, right? Enter the Samsung QS750F. For a relatively low MSRP of $899, the QS750F gives you a soundbar, two rears, and a subwoofer, which is considerably more generous than Sonos or JBL.

It has been revealed that as a result, the QS750F blows the competition out of the park. For under $1k, you get cinematic sound, with enviable width and immense bass. The QS750F sounds so good that we forgot we were supposed to be reviewing it.

Although it’s just a 5.1.2 channel configuration — considerably fewer speakers than JBL’s monstrous 1300XMK2, which boasts 11.1.4 channels and costs almost double — you probably wouldn’t be able to notice the difference.

SetupAs with every other soundbar, setup is a relatively quick process. Once the soundbar, subwoofer, and rears are unpackaged, simply connect everything to power and plug the soundbar into your TV using HDMI eARC.

Unlike JBL’s collection of premium soundbars, the QS750F’s rears aren’t truly “wireless” — sure, they connect to the soundbar wirelessly, but the left speaker must be connected to power. This is only an problem if you’re short on power outlets, extension cables, or if you want a particularly cable-free setup. Even so, you’re not going to get a better multi-speaker setup for less, so we think this is a worthy sacrifice.

It has been revealed that the subwoofer is wireless, so don’t worry about needing to connect that to the soundbar with a wire. It’ll automatically connect.

Sources indicate that how significant is itAs you might expect, the QS750F is a large soundbar. This is true of pretty much every high-power soundbar — they’re designed to be able to fill large rooms with both size and physical presence.

The soundbar is 46 inches long and ten inches deep, so you’ll need to ensure it fits on your TV stand/wall mount and that your TV is big enough. I’d recommend anything from 55 inches up.

It has been revealed that the subwoofer is effectively a 10 x 10 x 10-inch cube. We’d recommend positioning the subwoofer around 12 inches from the walls on all sides. You’ll need to play around with spacing to figure out the optimal position. Some setups come with configuration modes in the relevant app, but Samsung locks its proprietary Space Fit Pro behind post-2021 AI-powered Samsung TVs.

Industry observers note that are there any extrasThe QS750F comes with everything you need for a Dolby Atmos all-in-one setup. You get the soundbar, subwoofer, and two rears.

You also get AirPlay, Google Cast, and smart home features in the SmartThings app, which we’d recommend downloading. You can easily adjust playback modes and listening styles — movie, music, gaming, voice enhancement — to find what pleases you.

SoundAlright, now onto the most important part of any soundbar: its audio output. Thankfully, you’ll be pleased to know that the QS750F sounds utterly fantastic.

As the QS750F is a large soundbar, it’s intended for use in a large room. The side-firing speakers in the soundbar itself and the powerful subwoofer work together to create a wide soundscape worthy of a movie theater. Although there’s not as much height as width, the soundbar’s Dolby Atmos performance is still admirable.

It has been revealed that the dialogue performance is a clear standout, though: I was never left wondering what was being stated thanks to voice enhancement mode. This feature isolated dialogue well, and ensured even the moodiest and broodiest speech was crystal clear.

Most audiophiles will be the first to admit that soundbars aren’t ideal for playing music — me included — but the QS750F didn’t balk at the challenge. Although I’d much rather listen to music via my bookshelf speakers or headphones, the QS750F played every song with rich, pulsing bass, and would be good enough for a quick listening session or party.

In a recent development, sonos' compact soundbar brings excellent sound with a slightly higher price tag than the old model — but the app is still a bit tetchy. Still, this great-sounding bar is a great option for Sonos homes with living rooms too small for the Arc Ultra.

It has been revealed that the Sonos Beam Ultra feels like a statement of intent. The app works better than ever, the sound is incredible, and the surround sound straight out of the bar itself is top-notch. There are still problems — music sounds bad, and a lack of HDMI passthrough is a shame.

Recent findings suggest that but this is Sonos on top form. The design is great, bringing that Sonos minimalism to a smaller bar than the enormous Arc Ultra. It’s perhaps a little more plain than some of the brand's other devices, but it's a handsome thing that’ll blend in perfectly with any living room decor. The traditional black and white colorways are still the only options, unfortunately.

And then there’s the way it sounds. It increases the Dolby Atmos effect with height channels, making for a more immersive movie experience that lands you directly in the center of the action. Add in a few extra Sonos speakers for a full surround setup and you have the perfect movie-watching experience for a smaller space.

Sources indicate that it is expensive, mind you. The Beam was never cheap, but this one ups the price ante to make it a less compelling buy than other bars around this size class. And while Sonos app is much better than it was in early 2025, I’ve had more problems with it than our tester, with dropouts and other problems.

Setup is super easy. You just plug the soundbar into a wall outlet, and then an HDMI cable into the eARC port on the back of your TV. That could be it, if you’re not interested in any of the extra Sonos features.

In a recent development, to finish setup you’ll need to use the Sonos app, which is now much improved. From there you can do sound tuning setup amongst other things, like connecting extra Sonos surround speakers or a subwoofer for extra bass. It’s simple and easy to do, and the app will take you through it step by step.

This is also where you’ll stream audio to the device or adjust any settings. There’s no remote that comes with the soundbar — everything goes through the Sonos app.

The Beam Ultra really stretches the “compact” soundbar thing. It measures around 30 inches wide, making it a larger soundbar than some of the smaller compact options. That makes it perfect for TVs around 55 inches and smaller, though Sonos says it works for TVs up to 65 inches.

For larger spaces and TVs you’ll want the larger Sonos Arc Ultra.

In the box, you’ll find the soundbar, a power cable, and the HDMI cable. That’s it. There’s no remote, no wall mount — just the soundbar.

You can buy extras. Sonos speakers, the Era 100, 300, Sub Mini and Sub 4 all work as surround options for the Beam Ultra. I’d recommend the Era 100 and Sub Mini for smaller rooms if you want to increase the surround capability of the bar.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, everything has to come from Sonos’ rather enclosed ecosystem. You cannot add a separate 3rd-party subwoofer, for example. Shame.

According to recent reports, the Beam Ultra is the best Dolby Atmos soundbar for its size. There’s real height to the sound here, making for a far better immersive bubble than other similarly sized bars. There’s width too — it’s a great way to watch your favorite movies.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, stereo music sounds straight up bad. That’s a shame, given that Sonos nailed it with the Arc Ultra — if you want to listen to music, you’re better off grabbing a stereo pair of Era 100s. It’ll cost you less, too.

I've seen loads of soundbars pass over Tom's Guide's testing table, and while there are some excellent options out there, not all of them can fit onto one list.

That doesn't mean they're bad, by any stretch, and they might just be the best soundbar for you. Here are some of the soundbars that we liked testing but didn't quite make the cut for the main roundup.

It has been revealed that for the same money as Sonos's Beam Ultra, the Marshall Heston 60 is another compelling compact option. It might not quite reach the same heady heights as the Beam Ultra for movie watching, but it absolutely obliterates the Sonos when it comes to listening to music. It's just a shame that there aren't any surround speaker options.

Read our full Marshall Heston 60 review.

In a recent development, samsung's biggest and most premium sound is very good, offering excellent Dolby Atmos out of the box thanks to its included subwoofer and surround speakers. If you're looking for an all-in-one package for a Samsung TV it's a great option, but we believe the JBL equivalent offers a more rounded surround experience. If you're looking for the best soundbar surround sound, then look for the more expensive Sonos setup.

Read our full Samsung Q990H review.

This mid-range soundbar brings excellent sound, but it forgot to bring the premium price. You won't get any smart features, which is a shame, but when it sounds this good, you won't really care. The sub in the box is surprisingly strong for this price point, and the bar itself offers solid surround for the dollars you'll pay.

Read our full Samsung Q600F review.

The KEF XIO is one of the best-sounding soundbars we've ever tested. It's also one of the best-looking and best-built. "So why isn't it on the list!?" Because it costs $2,500. While I let that sink in for a second, I'll also tell you that the app experience is hit or miss. Still, if you have the dollars lying around, there are far worse ways to spend thousands of smackeroos.

LG's Sound Suite Dolby Atmos FlexConnect (phew) technology is very cool, and in the right room it can sound very good. Unfortunately, its core sound simply isn't up to scratch when compared to the competition, and the Sound Suite FlexConnect speakers are sold separately for a hefty premium. A proof of concept that shows its worth waiting for the sequel — but it needs some more time in the oven.

Read our full Sound Suite H7 review.

It has been revealed that the Polk Audio Signa S4 brings a great sound and surprisingly solid Dolby Atmos for a decent price. The included sub is plenty bassy, and there's good spaciousness to the sound. It's a large bar despite its lower price. The comprehensive remote control is comfortable and easy to use.

Read our full Polk Audio Signa S4 review.

Industry observers note that if you want something that looks super sleek and tidy, then the True X Bar is a great option. Its Dolby Atmos performance is admirable, and the price is right. We reviewed the 40A, but you can find the 50A for around the same price now. It's exactly the same, but comes with a subwoofer. But you can also buy the 40A and add a subwoofer later.

Read our full Yamaha True X Bar 40A review.

One of the best bits of most modern soundbars is that they're all simple to use in some form or another — but if you want something that you just plug in and use, then you'll want to avoid any with smart features.

While those smart features can make them sound better, or work for different types of content, they add complexity. An app might make it possible to access room EQs and the like, it also makes it more complicated for the end user.

Although we used to recommend avoiding Wi-Fi connections and apps if you just want to plug in and play, almost all soundbars now have some smart features. So I'd recommend looking for models that don't solely rely on those if the physical connection is your main focus.

First up, if your primary use case is music, go for a pair of speakers with an HDMI port like the Fluance Ri71. They sound much better than soundbars for music. You'll thank me later.

It has been revealed that now, for the other questions. TV customers will want something that increases dialoge clarity and makes it easier to hear what's going on in the news. You won't need a subwoofer or any kind of surround support. The Sony HT-S100F above is going to be perfect for you, given it's not too expensive and works great for TV.

Movie watchers should look out for subwoofers and surround speakers. You want more space for your Dolby Atmos mixes and the subwoofer will help with the low-end rumble you get with movies. The Sonos Arc Ultra and subwoofer is a good option for you, or the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 if you want something in one package.

If you have a small room or use a small TV, you don't want a massive soundbar; that much should be obvious. It wouldn't fit, for one, but it would also make your TV look much smaller. And who wants that.

However, you also don't want a soundbar that's too small for your TV. Otherwise, all of the sound will appear to come from the middle of the TV, rather than from it's sides like it should.

In a recent development, you'll want to get a decently sized soundbar if you've got something between 50-75 inches big. Larger than that and you should probably consider either the biggest soundbar you can lay your hands on, or a proper stereo setup built around one of the best home cinema receivers.

Jalen Brunson might be a pro at scoring baskets for the Fresh York Knicks, but now the NBA champ is helping shoppers score a different kind of win with Lowe’s Black Friday deals.

The superstar has teamed up with the home improvement retailer as an ambassador for its Black Friday campaign, which features hundreds of discounts on everything from tools to holiday decor and kitchen essentials. Better yet, Lowe’s is hosting a massive giveaway for shoppers willing to brave the crowds on the 27th.

And because this is the season of giving, there are even more bargains awaiting early shoppers. Why did Lowe’s feel like a natural partner to you?I feel like we embody a lot of the same qualities. One thing I grew up learning was the importance of serving others and helping people, and I feel like Lowe’s shares that same commitment. Our priorities align, so it felt natural to work with them.

He continued, “I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance. These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay.”.

Sources indicate that he then shifted focus to the White House and his ballroom, which has yet to be completed. “I want to commiserate with those Reporters and Citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House,” Trump noted. “It hasn’t been properly painted, or taken care of, for years. “They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again, but we won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands,” Trump affirmed. “We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!” Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 U2 Perform Dolly Parton's Final Recording During NFL Halftime Show Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys ⁠Gérard Depardieu to Face Trial for Allegedly Raping Actress Charlotte ⁠Arnould.

If you're on the lookout for a good deal on a portable projector, I recommend considering the following XGIMI deals.

Industry observers note that if you're looking for the most affordable option, the Vibe One projector is just $179 (originally $299) after a 40% discount. It already comes with Google TV, which is my favorite OS, so you can download and stream any app you want. If you have a bit more money to splurge, the MoGo 4 is the same concept as the Vibe One but takes its specs to the next level, and it's available starting at $359 (originally $499). It's still small and compact with 1080p resolution, but it nearly doubles the brightness, with 450 ISO lumens. The battery life more than doubles to two and a half hours in Eco Mode, while still keeping the projector under three pounds. It also has Google TV as its OS, but the projection is 360° with its adjustable built-in stand. You also have the option of getting the bundle with the PowerBase Stand, which extends the battery to five hours. Like the Vibe One, it has a built-in speaker, but this one uses dual 6W Harman Kardon speakers with Dolby Audio.The MoGo 4 Laser is a slightly upgraded version that uses triple laser technology for a better picture. It still supports 1080p resolution, but it's brighter with 550 ISO lumens and a 1000:1 contrast. The battery life, OS system, stand, speakers, and auto keystone technology are the same—but the bundles are different, so they're worth considering if they fit your needs.

If you're looking for a premium portable projector, the Horizon 30 Pro is a great option that competes with the best options on the market. It supports 4K resolution, uses RGB triple laser brightness that reaches 4800 ISO lumens (bright enough to see during the day), has a 120Hz refresh rate and gaming features to make gaming smooth, displays an 8,000:1 native contrast to make colors and blacks pop, and supports IMAX Enhanced, Dolby Vision, and HDR10+. It has an adjustable stand like the other XGIMI projectors and its own dual 12W Harman Kardon speakers with DTS Virtual:X and DTS-HD. The auto keystone is just as powerful as the other options, but the lens adds an optical zoom and a Lens Memory feature, which lets you save up to six custom lens and image setups and recall them with a click. Right now, it's down to $1,899 (originally $2,499) after a 24% discount.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Denmark’s TV2 has dipped into the independent production market for an Acting Program Director as it seeks penance over the scandal around Truman Show-like reality series Everybody Loves Rasmus.

Sune Roland will take up the position on December 1, and will lead the TV2 programming division during a period the network “is working to rebuild the Danish public’s trust.” Given his position is an acting role, it’s not certain he will be TV2’s long-term program chief just yet.

Recent findings suggest that this follows the departures of Content Director Ulla Pors and Program Director Dorthe Thirstrup following the disastrous launch of Alle Elsker Rasmus (Everybody Loves Rasmus). Related Stories News Content Chiefs At Denmark's TV2 Step Down To "Restore Trust" After Backlash Over 'Truman Show'-Style Reality Series News Banijay Takes On Norway's 'The Comedy League'.

It has been revealed that the show faced immense public backlash for duping comedian Rasmus Wallbridge into believing his dream film concept was being produced. It was scrapped soon after launch, and TV2’s directors have launched an investigation into how the show was greenlit in the first place. Their response has been fast and decisive during in an almost unprecedented situation for a major European broadcaster. Watch on Deadline.

Roland is a former TV2 exec, having risen as high as Head of Content, and returns after four years in the independent production sector. He had worked as Managing Director of Strong Productions, the Fremantle Denmark production house that merged with Blu last year. Following his exit there, he launched his own manufacturer, Shift Studios.

According to recent reports, frederik Lauesen, who was installed as Acting Content Director at TV2 in the aftermath of the scandal, said: “I am very pleased that Sune Roland has agreed to take on the role of Acting Programme Director. Sune brings extensive experience; he is well-liked and respected within the industry and possesses a deep understanding of both TV 2 and the Danish production landscape. He is a highly skilled professional and an accomplished leader, and we will greatly benefit from his expertise in the time ahead.”.

Lauesen said TV2 was facing “a serious situation” and that rebuilding trust was paramount. “We must address this while continuing to manage a large and diverse portfolio of content – an effort we carry out in close collaboration with our talented colleagues in the programming department and the Danish production industry. Sune’s experience from both sides of the table will prove valuable in the time ahead.”.

Recent findings suggest that roland acknowledged he was joining in “particularly challenging times,” but added: TV2 holds a special place for me, and I know how many talented and dedicated people work every day to create content that truly matters to the Danish public. I look forward to contributing my experience and collaborating with both colleagues and production companies.”.

Roland worked as TV2’s Head of Factual between 2007 and 2011, and then from 2012 until 2022 held roles such as Head of Programming, Channel Head, and Head of Content. He has also held senior leadership positions at Koncern TV and Metronome Productions.

TV2 will begin a recruitment process for a “future leadership team within the programming division” at a later date.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler claims that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

According to recent reports, I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler notes, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting manufacturer to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

It has been revealed that the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

I test dozens of workout headphones every year and these are the 6 sets I recommend right now

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when you're pumping weights or running a marathon, you're going to want something to keep your mind occupied — and there's little better than the best workout headphones.
  • Sources indicate that there are loads of options out there, but some are better than others.
  • Sources indicate that we've tested plenty more of course, and we've tested as many as we can.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when you're pumping weights or running a marathon, you're going to want something to keep your mind occupied — and there's little better than the best workout headphones. Listen to music, catch up with your favorite podcast, or devour some of an audiobook. Whatever you're doing you'll need some buds.

Sources indicate that there are loads of options out there, but some are better than others. Our favorites are the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, with their great sound perfectly pairing with solid ANC and a comfortable fit.

Sources indicate that we've tested plenty more of course, and we've tested as many as we can. So read on to find out which headphones you should be getting for your next sweat-proof listening session.

AI seems to be the latest fitness trend, popping up in smartwatches, workout apps, and headphones. I wouldn't recommend picking up a fresh pair of earbuds for these features. My experience is the AI functions aren't very useful, and will likely change a lot in the next few years. So, focus on finding a set that feel and sound good, allowing you to focus on your exercise without distraction.

For a long time, Beats headphones didn't make me think of exercise. But that was before Apple redesigned the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 in early 2025 into what are effectively AirPods for workouts, with active noise cancellation (ANC), an effective transparency mode, and proper support for iPhone and Android devices.

The winged design of the older Powerbeats Pro has been replaced with over-ear hooks, which are a lot more stable. I'd sometimes need to fiddle a bit to get them on, but once locked into place, they didn't budge. And because the hook keeps some of the weight out of your ear, they were comfortable to wear for hours at a time.

It has been revealed that though the downside of this design is that the case is pretty massive, and much larger than you'd comfortably fit into leggings or a pocket; fine for throwing in a gym bag, less ideal for carrying about, unlike the minuscule Beats Solo Buds case. But this one tops the battery up to 45 hours, while the Solo Buds case is just for storage.

Recent findings suggest that the Powerbeats Pro 2 come with Apple's H2 chip, just like the AirPods Pro 3, so expect similar speedy performance, although I didn't find the noise cancellation or transparency mode were quite up to the flagship buds' standard. Though I did jump with delight at the use of physical buttons on each bud.

These headphones powered me through weights workouts, meditation sessions and long outdoor walks with no concerns. I put them in and they did exactly what I wanted; good audio with no fuss. I don't run, but my coworker Nick Harris-Fry does, and found the Powerbeats Pro 2 a good companion for runs too.

Recent findings suggest that the company leaned heavily into the buds' heart rate monitor at launch. It's neat, but you'll probably never use it. There's a small optical sensor built into the buds which is used to track your heart rate during workouts, but if this is something you care about, you likely have a smartwatch or Garmin watch that can do this better.

If you’re looking for some top-notch earbuds for working out that won’t break the bank, then look no further than the CMF By Nothing Buds 2. With loads of gym-centric features at a price that’s less than a fifth of some of the more expensive options on the list, they’re a fantastic way to keep fit while listening to tunes. Or a podcast. Or like, white noise. Whatever floats your workout boat.

At this price point, you wouldn’t expect to find anything with noise canceling, let alone ANC that works this well. It did a great job of keeping a noisy office at bay, so the pounding techno in the gym will be no problem. Outdoor runners, rejoice, they also blocked out traffic sounds when our tester, Ashley, took them out for a walk.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears destroying them either, thanks to IP55 water resistance. You won’t be able to wear them while swimming, but anything you might get up to around your block or at the gym is no problem at all. Music, come rain or shine.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t even have to worry about them running out of juice mid-workout. The quoted battery life from CMF is 12 hours — we found that around 5 hours of use left us with 60% remaining. Add in the 55 hours in the case, and you’re home free for super lengthy sessions.

They’re a little cheap-looking and the environmental noise canceling in calls is… not great. But then you look at your bank balance, realize that choosing the cheaper earbuds has left you with spare cash for a better gym subscription, and suddenly everything seems to make sense again.

It has been revealed that they go in your ears, stay there, and play music while you get on with your workout. Better yet, they’ve done it for less than just about anything else around. What more could you want?

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are the follow-up to our former favorite running headphones, the OpenRun Pro. These bone conduction headphones sound great, despite the fact they use vibrations on your cheeks to transmit audio.

While out running with the OpenRun Pro 2 (or most Shokz headphones for that matter), we found that the fit was comfortable and secure, so you won't need to continually fiddle with them and can focus on your training.

The downside to the headband-style design is that you can't adjust the fit. However, there's a smaller edition (OpenRun Pro 2 Mini) that has a shorter band for improved fit. But we were impressed with the comfort during runs, bike rides, and yoga sessions.

You don't get a charging case, but we found that the battery would last around 12 hours between top-ups, which should see you through most workouts. That said, if you like to dial up the volume to max, expect closer to 10 hours of power.

I'm not a runner, but my multi-marathoner coworker Nick Harris-Fry summed up his feelings on the headphones, concluding: "They’re my preferred running headphones at the moment because of the excellent fit, open design and good sound. If you just want running headphones with an open design, it’s the OpenRun Pro 2.".

They can survive sweaty workouts and light rain, but if you plan to train in the wet or want a more multi-functional set that'll cope with a dip in the pool, the OpenSwim Pro are a good alternative, and they have onboard MP3 storage.

According to recent reports, the AirPods Pro 3 are Apple's newest flagship headphones, and stuffed with more features than ever. There's live translation, voice isolation on calls and head gestures to control your phone. All of that's great, but it's the fitness features that really stand out.

Like the Powerbeats Pro 2, the AirPods Pro 3 now have built-in heart rate sensors. Unlike the Beats set at launch, you can actually use the sensors with a load of different apps, including (importantly) Apple Fitness.

The new integration with Apple Fitness adds Workout Buddy, an AI-powered 'coach' which sends you motivational messages and performance stats, like an audio-only version of what you'd find on the Apple Watch Series 12.

I'm generally skeptical about features like this, but our resident marathon runner, Nick Harris-Fry, actually seemed impressed with the heart rate accuracy, which informs a lot of the performance metrics on Workout Buddy and Apple Fitness.

Then there's the fit. Despite being popular workout earbuds, I've always found that AirPods need quite a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But that's not the case with the redesigned tip here, which Fitness Editor Jane McGuire remarked performed brilliantly on runs.

Sources indicate that despite being one of the first mainstream brands to launch water-resistant phones, the AirPods Pro 2 were surprisingly vulnerable, with just an IPX4 rating, essentially for splashes. The Pro 3 upgrade to a much hardier IP57 for dust and water resistance, so you can finally use them in the elements.

Like the AirPods Pro 2 before, the Pro 3 are still disappointing on the battery front: eight hours per bud, up to 24 hours with the case (while you got 30 out of the case on the Pro 2). It's not terrible, but the sub-$50 CMF By Nothing Buds 2 reach 12 hours.

It has been revealed that the main reason I don't rate these higher in the list of best workout headphones is mostly due to the design — these aren't made for sports and they're not as secure a fit as you'd need for all high-intensity workouts. But for general use with your iPhone, including yoga, HIIT sessions, and casual runs, they're a great choice.

As Google continues to develop the Pixel-branded ecosystem of devices to rival Apple's iPhone and AirPods, it's no surprise that the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are the best workout headphones for Android, even if they are targeted squarely at owners of the brand's range of Pixel phones.

The key upgrade from the first-generation Pixel Buds Pro is the addition of Google Gemini, the brand's generative AI model. As it's still fairly new, it doesn't replace the older virtual Google Assistant, although in theory it can. But in practice, we found that it doesn't always offer the most accurate answers.

In a recent development, features like voice assistants and hands-free controls are useful, but not essential when you're working out. Instead, it's more key that they stay in place as you exercise. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have a upcoming wing on each bud to help them lock into your ears.

Industry observers note that this would be great, but it doesn't quite reach the inner-top part of your ear, so we still found a bit of adjustment was needed to keep them in position for optimal noise cancellation. Google also claims to have improved the ANC, but it's hard to really tell the difference between the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and the original.

It has been revealed that however, it's still effective, blocking out most noises except for some higher frequency sounds like crying babies and emergency service sirens. The sound quality matches the Pixel Buds Pro, although you may want to tweak the EQ to your preferences, as the default setting is a bit heavy on the lower end.

It has been revealed that one other thing they have in common with the AirPods Pro is that they're not necessarily the best workout headphones if you spend hours training every week, as the fit isn't quite optimized for high-impact exercise. But if you're after a versatile option to wear at the gym and at the office, the Pixel Buds Pro 2 are a great choice.

Industry observers note that bone conduction headphones are cool, but they’re bulky. Your common earbuds sound great, but they have a habit of making it difficult to hear your surroundings. Open earbuds, like the Beyerdynamic Amiron Zero, are a great middle ground that offer solid sound while allowing you to hear the rogue bus that’s bearing down on you as you do your morning run.

According to recent reports, they’re surprisingly secure, their silicone “hinges” holding onto your outer ear with little discomfort and no wiggle. Ashley, our tester, had no problem wearing them for hours and hours on end, partly thanks to their lightweight design. Just remember that these are completely open, playing the sound at your ears rather than in. Everyone is going to hear your playlist. Everyone.

In a recent development, the battery life could be better. There are 20 hours total on tap here, which falls down compared to in-ear options. You’ll be reaching for the charging cable more often than not, unfortunately, although you won’t need to pop them in the charging case as often with 6 hours of realistic listening time. Our tests pretty much confirmed this number.

Sound-wise, these are a great alternative to in-ear buds. There’s less bass than we might like overall, but there’s little else we’d ask for. The mids sound good, and the treble is solid as well. Don’t expect game-changing audio, but for open buds these sound great.

Even better, you can change the EQ. That’s a major bonus for something like this, and it means you can change the sound to your heart's content so that they sound great no matter your sonic preference. Five bands of adjustment, baby.

They’re IP54 water- and dust-resistant too, so you don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears causing any problems down the line. These are a good pair of earbuds that open you up to safer, more aware exercise — we really like them.

According to recent reports, the workout headphones in the guide above aren't the only ones we've tested. We regularly try out workout earbuds so that we can recommend the top options that are worth spending your hard-earned cash on.

Recent findings suggest that however, there are several other good options if you're after a bit more choice. These are the earbuds we've tested that didn't quite make the cut.

I really, really like these headphones. They're almost the perfect version of Beats' workout headphones, but the fit (ahem) isn't always perfect, and when they're only $50 less than the much more stable Powerbeats Pro 2 with fewer features and worse battery life, you're better off with the Pro 2.

Read our full Beats Powerbeats Fit review.

The OpenFit Air 2 are great open earbuds, featuring solid sound and a comfortable fit. What holds them back from a full mention on the list is the fiddli-ness of the ear hooks — the clip-on design is superior if you're looking for something both secure and easy to wear.

Read our full Shokz OpenFit Air 2 review.

It has been revealed that when Apple released these in mid-2024, I loved them, even though they didn't have noise cancellation or a charging case. But now these are only marginally cheaper than the much better Powerbeats Fit, and about the same price as the more feature-packed CMF By Nothing Buds 2, it's hard to recommend them.

Read our full Beats Solo Buds review.

The JBL SoundGear Sense have an open-ear design, so they sit on top of your ears rather than in them. We found this was fine for quiet environments or working out at home, but as soon as there was a lot of background noise from wind or traffic, it'd easily drown out the audio. They're comfortable and durable, but best-suited to indoor exercise.

Read our full JBL SoundGear Sense review.

Industry observers note that before investing your money in a set of workout headphones, you want to be sure that they do what they claim and are comfortable enough to wear during your training. That's why we put each set to the test before including it in the guide.

I've been testing headphones for almost ten years and know the most vital areas to check out before recommending any pair. You really don't want them to fall out and get lost or need to continually adjust them in your ears.

So, we wear the headphones across a range of training styles, including high-impact runs (which can cause a lot of vibration and movement), intense fast-paced workouts and weightlifting sessions to see how they fare.

If they easily stay in place, they glide through this test, but it's not a write-off if they do move — headphones that struggle with runs may still make great weights companions — so we move into other areas, like comfort and sound.

For longer sessions, including runs, yoga classes and extended gym sessions, we check that the headphones are actually comfortable in your ears and don't leave you with ear pain or pressure headaches, which can happen with some sets.

Likewise, you don't want them to run out of battery mid-session, so we check how the battery life stacks up to the manufacturer's specs. For earbuds, we see how long they last out of the case and confirm how long the case can boost that.

Sources indicate that when it comes to sound quality, even the best workout headphones aren't going to be a match for the best audiophile headphones in terms of clarity and detail. But that doesn't mean you need to put up with poor or low-quality audio.

We use a consistent playlist of music to help compare the headphones to other sets we've tested, which includes a variety of motivational dance music, dynamic rock songs, and everything in between, including the best fresh workout music.

There are a lot of Bluetooth workout headphones out there, so it can be a challenge to decide between them all. However, there are a few considerations to keep in mind that'll help narrow your options down to the right ones for your needs.

Firstly, it's vital that they stay in place during your exercise sessions. Some have ear hooks to physically hold them down, but others rely on clever engineering, a range of ear tips, or a specific set of materials to stop them falling out.

You also want them to survive some degree of moisture. If you blueprint to get sweaty, then you'll need a set rated to at least IPX4 for water resistance. But for outdoor workouts with a chance of rain, it's best to aim for an IPX7 rating.

Sources indicate that importantly, they also need to last the length of your workout. If you're doing short, high-intensity sessions, then you may only need an hour of battery. But with the right case, you may only need to recharge them every couple of weeks.

If long runs are more your thing or you're training for a marathon, you'll need a long-lasting set, like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2, which are specifically designed with long distance outdoor runners in mind and last up to 12 hours.

And, finally, how loud do you like your workouts? If you don't mind some background noise at the gym, then a set of passive noise-canceling headphones should do the job, but most of the best workout earbuds have active noise cancellation (ANC) instead.

Earbuds with ANC cancel out the sound before it even hits your ears, so they're ideal if you want to zone out to your favorite tracks and focus on your exercise. But you may also want to hear traffic when you're out and about, so choose a set with a transparency mode too, which cancels most, but not all, noise.

According to recent reports, in mid-2025, I had to do something hard; say goodbye to the Jabra Elite 8 Active. These were my favorite workout earbuds, but Jabra decided to focus only on business audio and no longer makes consumer earbuds or headphones.

In a recent development, I'd been using Jabra's Elite Active headphones since 2019, and for more than half a decade they comfortably sat atop my list of the best workout headphones. But we move. Times have changed, and they're gone (but still supported, for now).

You'd struggle to find a latest pair now as most retailers have run down their supplies, but if you're after new workout earbuds, and to my mind, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a worthy successor (even if they do add an ear hook).

Recent findings suggest that if you've been hunting for new workout headphones, you may have noticed that each set has an IP rating for water resistance. This stands for Ingress Protection, and it's a measure of how well the buds can stand dirt and water.

Sources indicate that there's a standard format to the rating — IPXY — where X refers to the level of dust protection and Y relates to the device's water resistance. The dust protection runs from 0 to 6, while water ranges between 0 and 9.

Unless you're working out in very dusty environments, the dust protection is less relevant and most brands don't even test them against that part of the standard. Instead, you'll want to pay attention to the water rating.

Industry observers note that headphones with an IPX4 rating are protected against water, so will cope with sweaty workouts. However, if you want to run in the rain (or are worried about getting caught in a storm) then aim for a set with an IPX7 rating.

Sources indicate that this means they can be submerged in water up to 1 meter deep for 30 minutes without damage. That doesn't mean you should take them swimming (you'll want some waterproof headphones for that) but dropping them in a puddle isn't going to do them any harm.

Our roundup only includes workout earbuds, but it's not uncommon to see some people train with over-ear headphones instead, especially at the gym. So, which should you wear for exercise?

According to recent reports, ultimately, it comes down to preference, but there are a few factors to consider. Over-ears use an adjustable headband to keep them in place, so they're not likely to move about, especially if you're lifting weights.

Sources indicate that even just a few years ago, in-ear buds weren't really designed with exercise in mind, so they'd often fall out or need a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But the best workout headphones we've included here all have ways to overcome that challenge.

Some, like the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, have ear hooks to hold them securely, while others use a combination of weight balance and grippy materials to prevent them falling from your ear mid-workout.

But many people also feel like a larger set of headphones will have longer battery life and sound better too. However, the performance gap has shrunk, so you can get impressive noise cancellation and battery life from workout earbuds now.

The downside to over-ears is that they're generally not designed for sweaty exercise. Many have leather ear pads, and these swiftly wear with repeated movements and contact with sweat. You can replace them, but it's not ideal.

The earbuds are also lighter, so you're less likely to notice you have them in, while over-ear cans can start to press against your skull and contribute to tension headaches, unless they're specifically designed for comfort. Although that usually makes them less durable.

Sources indicate that generally, no. This is partly due to the intricate designs required to make small earbuds packed with batteries, sensors, and headphone components. But it's also because most brands don't prioritize repairability.

Industry observers note that many sets, like those in our best workout headphones roundup, are durable, so shouldn't get easily damaged. And since most offer some degree of water resistance, a bit of sweat or light rain shouldn't cause you any problems.

In a recent development, so any significant damage is going to come from accidents, like dropping a weight onto an errant bud. However, you may notice a drop in battery life in the longer term, which you usually can't do anything about.

The only way around this would be to pick up a set of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2, which may be the world's most repairable earbuds since you can replace seven parts, including the battery and outer shell.

All of the sets in our best workout headphones roundup are wireless and connect to your smartphone or other devices via Bluetooth. But you can still find wired sets, including the Apple EarPods, which look a bit like AirPods but with a cable and Lightning connector to plug into your iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that wired sets also tend to be cheaper, so you may be considering a set that you wouldn't need to worry as much about damaging or replacing. However, it's crucial to consider how you like to train before picking up a wired set.

Recent findings suggest that to keep them connected, you'll need to have your phone somewhere on your body, either in a pocket, waistband or running phone holder. Consequently, there are two different devices moving at different times as you exercise; your earphones and your smartphone.

The movements are translated between them with the cable, so if you stretch your leg out, the cable tenses and may tug on your earphones, which could lead to them falling out.

Plus, if you're working out with weights or other equipment, there's also the risk that the wire will get tangled up, leading to the headphones falling out or the cable getting ripped.

Similarly, if you prefer to keep aware of your surroundings, you can use most wireless workout headphones in mono mode, with just a single earbud in while the other stays in the case. You don't have the same option for wired workout headphones.

Industry observers note that many runners would advise picking up a set of the best bone conduction headphones for running. Like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 in our roundup, these use vibrating pads on your cheekbones to reproduce audio, leaving your ears free to pick up the sounds around you, like traffic and other people.

This is very helpful while out running, especially if you want to run safely in the dark. Although music can be a great motivator, you don't want to miss notable alerts like emergency vehicle sirens or bikes coming up behind you.

Sources indicate that plus, it means that you're more aware of everything else going on around you, including other runners and pedestrians. And if you plan to run races, using bone conduction headphones allows you to chat with other runners and listen to music.

You can get similar effects with most of the best workout headphones, as transparency modes use the earbuds' built-in mics to elevate environmental noise, but bone conduction headphones also wrap around your head, so stay in place more effectively during high-impact activities like running.

It has been revealed that if you want to prevent your earbuds falling out of your ears or slipping out of place, the first thing to consider if the type of exercise you want to do. For running and other high-impact activities like jumping, the most secure type of workout headphones are those with ear hooks.

According to recent reports, these sit above your ear to prevent them moving or falling out, and so can cope more effectively with vibrations. This is also why many runners opt for a set of the best bone conduction headphones, since these wrap around your head to similar effect.

If you want more minimalist earbuds, then before you start your workout, you can adjust the silicone ear tips. Most sets come with a small, medium, and large replacement pair of tips so you can find the ones that fit your ear size the most.

According to recent reports, in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

Industry observers note that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

It has been revealed that chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Latest York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

In a recent development, the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
