📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ariana Grande may be one of the biggest pop stars in the world, but she’s also a true multi-hyphenate, known for her uncanny impressions and acting chops. Grande can hit a killer vocal run, produce a sleek beat, and steal a scene with terrific comedic timing. (It’s called range.) Her Hollywood career has grown with her pop star status — she started as a Broadway baby, singing her heart out in the musical 13, and eventually became one of Nickelodeon’s most beloved airheads as she played Cat Valentine on Victorious.

Industry observers note that now, she’s starring alongside Robert De Niro in the upcoming movie Focker-In-Law, which is out this week. So what better time to look back at the roles that have helped the megastar get to this point? Here are some of her most impressive moments both on the significant and small screens.

Part of what makes Grande’s acting career so much fun to watch is that she never does what anyone is expecting her to do — and she’s not above extreme silliness. That makes her Zoolander 2 performance particularly entertaining. It’s extremely brief, but she pops on-screen just in time to have a wild orgy with Hansel (Owen Wilson). The scene marked her first time meeting Ben Stiller, who she reunites with in Focker-In-Law. She looked back at their meet-cute fondly during a recent appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon: “He was directing me in an orgy scene in Zoolander 2 with a hippo and Susan Sarandon,” she shared. “So right off the bat, we had a comfortability.” —Julyssa Lopez.

Industry observers note that grande is one of the best parts of Adam McKay’s 2021 satire Don’t Look Up. She plays Riley Bina, a major pop star who is out-of-touch with the world — and the fact that a humanity-ending comet is headed Earth’s way. Once people start believing PhD student Kate Dibiasky (Jennifer Lawrence) and her advisor Dr. Randall Mindy (Leonardo DiCaprio) about their chilling prediction, Bina performs her new song “Just Look Up” with her cheating boyfriend, DJ Chello (Kid Cudi). The scene finds Grande delivering killer one-liners like, “Listen to the goddamn qualified scientists, we really fucked it up this time” while suspended onstage and sporting a ridiculous get-up of white feathers. According to McKay, many of the song’s lyrics were improvised by Grande. —Maya Georgi.

Industry observers note that in 2013, Nickelodeon adapted Gordon Korman’s 2008 novel Swindle, shaping it into a made-for-television heist movie revolving around two friends who set out to recover a $1.2 million baseball card. They form an unlikely group with other kids from their school harboring secret skills, and Grande steps in as a cheerleader with an undercover geeky side. The film came during her Sam & Cat days, and teamed her up with co-star Jennette McCurdy, while also letting her go beyond her flaky Cat persona. —J.L.

Industry observers note that when Grande reprises the role of Glinda for the second half of the Wicked tale, she’s planning her wedding to Prince Fiyero, all of Emerald City idolizes her, and everything is as she always wished — or is it? As Glinda reevaluates her life and decides to change paths to help her friend Elphaba (Cynthia Erivo), there are fewer of the rollicking comedy moments that made Grande’s performance in the first film so fun to watch. But with major songs like “I Couldn’t Be Happier,” “The Girl in the Bubble,” and the booming duet “For Good,” she makes clear why she was a natural fit for the iconic role. —Kate Storey.

Guest-starring on the campy horror-comedy television show Scream Queens as Chanel #2 was Ariana Grande’s first adult role after leaving Nickelodeon’s Sam & Cat to focus on her music. Creator Ryan Murphy said in 2015 that initially, Grande “was just going to do one episode, but she loved the process so much that she wanted to do more.” Even though she played a corpse in a few of those episodes, Ari’s comedic skills shine through, especially in a scene where her character’s ghost visits Emma Roberts’ Chanel #1. Grande is hilarious when speaking about her afterlife in hell. Whether her character is that she’s in a bad mood because Adolf Hitler was motorboating her boobs or that Jesus broke into heaven and stole the dinosaurs, she steals every scene. —Alison Weinflash.

Let’s look beyond the fact that Cat Valentine seemingly has a legitimate lobotomy in the middle of the Victorious run. There would not be an Ariana Grande without the exposure, preparation, and genuine war stories that the cast ofVictorious went through. While the will-they-won’t-they nature of Cat’s relationship with Robbie (Matt Bennett) was finally resolved in the apocalyptic music video for “One Last Time,” the most memorable musical moments of the series all involved Grande: from the karaoke bar rendition of “Give it Up” to the “They didn’t say I couldn’t sing” riff on the Victorious iCarly collab “Leave It All to Shine.” As Cat, Grande earned her place in the Hollywood Arts High School hall of fame and started her path toward becoming a household name. —C.T. Jones.

In a recent development, ariana Grande has hosted SNL three times now, and she always makes her appearances memorable by leveraging her exceptional impersonation skills, showcasing her comedy agility, and refusing to shy away from being wildly silly. We’ve seen her play Jennifer Lawrence during a Family Feud recreation and playing a shy intern who saves her radio station with her ability to sound like everyone from Shakira to Celine Dion. But her most beloved contributions might be in an off-key bridesmaid in the famed Domingo skit and giving us a hilarious take on Home Alone. —J.L.

Sources indicate that grande’s character in Focker In Law, Olivia Jones, is a multi-hyphenate not unlike the actress who portrays her. Just swap the gold records for FBI credentials, throw in vegan cooking chops, and you have a future in-law (to grandpa Jack Byrnes, reprised brilliantly by Robert De Niro) hell-bent on entering the “circle of trust” in record time. Grande plays the ultra-competitive Liv with exacting comedic timing, offering the perfect foil for Ben Stiller’s goofball insecurity. —Shirley Halperin.

According to recent reports, it takes self-determination, drive, and a lot of pink to make the world’s most coveted role your own. Ariana Grande wasn’t the frontrunner when Universal first unveiled it would be making a Wicked film. But the Petal singer fought to claim Glinda’s glitter wand. “Oz has been my safe space for as long as I can remember,” she wrote in an open letter to fans before the film’s premiere. It’s hard to imagine a world where the gleeful shrieks of Grande’s “Popular” outro didn’t exist — and her participation in the John M. Chu duology is a career-defining moment, proof the former Nick star is never far from her musical theater roots. —C.T.J.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a major change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

The iPhone 17e was released in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

Recent findings suggest that the current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

  • Industry observers note that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off.
  • With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

Industry observers note that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

In a recent development, simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically patch across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

Recent findings suggest that iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

Sources indicate that the biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. At the moment, just three carriers support the feature:.

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon states it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no looks to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

It has been revealed that in my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Industry observers note that have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

Sources indicate that THANKSGIVING AM UPGRADE: An alpha female property, Lionsgate‘s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping with a continued 5-day forecast of $85M+, is stealing business from two other female-leaning movies at the Thanksgiving box office, Universal/Paramount’s Focker In-Law and Disney’s Hexed, both of which are coming in lighter than their forecasts with 5-days of $36M and $35M respectively. That’s essentially a fight for 2nd over the Wednesday-Sunday stretch at this point in time.

Sources indicate that now, that’s not to say that it was silly to date other female pics on top of another tentpole, however, the holiday has shown that two exceptionally pleasing events for the demo can coexist at the same time, read 2024’s Moana 2 and Wicked and even last year’s Wicked: For Good and Zootopia 2. Hexed and Focker In-Law aren’t exceptionally pleasing.

Most movies are expected to ease on average -23% today off their Wednesday daily B.O. as families ease back for festivities. Tomorrow, Black Friday, should see a daily surge between 50%-100% for most titles. Watch on Deadline.

Sunrise on the Reaping‘s $15.1M Wednesday is the second best in the Suzanne Collins’ franchise after 2013’s Catching Fire which did $20.8M on the day before Thanksgiving. 3-day is still on track for $58M+, -51%.

Focker In-Law saw an uptick in its franchise CinemaScore to B+ from previous chapter, 2010’s Little Fockers which received a B-. The original movie 26 years ago has the best grade of A-. The pic is alright with a 64% definite recommend in Screen Engine/Rentrak PostTrak exits. Yesterday was $5.3M with the 3-day at $24.8M. Half of the audience was 18-34 yesterday, 46% over 35 and 64% female overall. Diversity demos were 37% Caucasian, 33% Latino and Hispanic, 13% Black, 10% Asian American and 7% Native American/other. PLFs rep 17% of the gross so far with the John Hamburg directed sequel (the first two pics were helmed by Jay Roach, the third by Paul Weitz) playing best in the West, South, and South Central. AMC Burbank is the top venue with $21k. Again, the Uni and Paramount co-production cost $90M net before global P&A.

Industry observers note that disney’s $200M Hexed is waiting for a box office spell tomorrow that could raise this original animated movie above the doldrums of the studio’s Thanksgiving 2023 dud Wish ($175M production cost, $8.1M Wednesday, $19.6M 3-day, $31.6M 5-day and final domestic of $63.9M). Hexed made $7.6M yesterday (including Tuesday previews) and is eyeing a 3-day of $20M. Hexed gets an A- just like Wish did. PostTrak shows 62% definite recommend for the general audience while kids under 12 gave it a 96% in the top 2 and a 51% must see right away. Kids under 12 rep 31% of the audience while 35-44 (parents) indicated up at 31%. Diversity demos were 48% Caucasian, 26% Latino and Hispanic, 9% Black, 7% Asian American and 9% Native American/other.

Again, there are no original songs in this movie about a mother and daughter witch, the latter who realizes her powers as both are transported into another portal where they are trying to save their own kind from doom.

Like Focker-in-Law, Hexed is sharing PLFs with Sunrise on the Reaping which owns most of the holiday supply, those screens are counting 17% of the animated pic’s holiday B.O. so far. 3D is driving 12%. West, South, South Central, Midwest and Mountain are the best markets with the East soft performing 2% below the norm this week. AMC Dine-In Disney Springs Florida is the best location with $52k.

Paramount’s Ebenezer is looking at 4th place at 3,180 theaters with $1.6M yesterday, and still $6.8M-$7.3M third weekend, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s I Play Rocky with $1.4M yesterday at 2,711 sites, $6.6M 3-day, -29%, 5-day of $9.6M and total of $22.6M by EOD Sunday.

Industry observers note that outside the top 5 is Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 252 locations, boosted by AMC Imax. Wednesday’s opening day estimate was $910K, 3-day is looking at $3.3M and a 5-day of $4.85M. At that level, the theater average over 5-days is $19,2K which is higher than what Netflix pulled did last Thanksgiving with Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery which had a per theater of $7K. Note that Rian Johnson directed thriller was booked in more theaters at 600 sites. Still a bit more robust result here on a limited basis than Wake Up Dead Man ($4.25M 5-day), but alas, Netflix, you’re leaving soooo much money on the table and there’s more than a enough room in this marketplace to have gone wide and minted at least $20M for this sequel to beloved fan Quentin Tarantino pic Once Upon a Time in Hollywood which at $142.8M is the Oscar winning filmmaker’s second highest grossing movie at the domestic B.O. Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher told Collider that the pic cost $120M-$123M, not $200M. We’ll leave it to Wall Street to figure out the downstream.

There’s a shot that Neon’s third weekend wide expansion of James Gray’s crime noir, Paper Tiger, based on the filmmaker’s life, comes in higher than Cliff Booth. Wednesday was an estimated $950K which translates into a $4.4M 3-day, 5-day of $5.1M at 1,322 (+1,294) theaters. Running total by Sunday is around $5.7M. Audiences weren’t wild about the Miles Teller, Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson movie giving it a C+.

Angel Studio’s Hershey biopic about the chocolate maker with Alexandra Daddario and Finn Whitlock got a leg up with early shows yesterday with $1.3M including $534K estimated previews. No firm projection yet, but it was always expected to file in the single digits over its ‘4-day’ start. The pic doesn’t officially open until Thursday and all that preview cash will be rolled into day one. CinemaScore audiences love it with an A, and PostTrak isn’t shabby with 83% positive and a 69% definite recommend, but critics didn’t have a sweet tooth for it 17% Rotten. Male-to-female turnout was 50/50 with the Angel faithful attending at 37% over 55, and 51% over 45. Diversity demos are 61% Caucasian, 17% Black, 13% Latino and Hispanic, 6% Asian American, and 3% Native American/other.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON: If extreme weather doesn’t shutter theaters in the Northeast, then Lionsgate is looking forward to a lucrative Thanksgiving stretch with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping potentially banking $85M+ over five-days.

Should the sixth title in the Suzanne Collins series file in that range, it will rep the second best Thanksgiving haul for a Hunger Games movie after Catching Fire‘s $109.9M Wednesday-Sunday turkey take 13 years ago. Sunrise on the Reaping‘s Wednesday is looking like $15.5M-$16.5M with a second 3-day weekend around $58M-$65M at 4,018 theaters, -46% to -51%. Five day forecasts are always a challenge for the industry to predict: Business dips on Thanksgiving then spikes on Black Friday, which is one of the most active moviegoing days of the year. By Sunday, we’re looking at a running cume for the Francis Lawrence directed movie of $233M domestic, which would be 40% higher than the lifetime cume on 2023’s Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

Second will either be Disney’s Hexed at 3,725 theaters or Universal/Paramount’s Focker-in-Law at 3,382 sites. Hexed is seeing around $7.8M today (including $2.1M previews), for a 3-day around $20M and 5-day between $35M-$40M. Let’s see if this picks up before passing complete judgement on this $200M original animation production, but it’s clear Hexed isn’t Coco or Frozen.

Sources indicate that focker In-Law is seeing a $5.2M Wednesday, 3-day of $24.8M and 5-day of $36.1M. No Rotten Tomatoes audience scores yet on either title.

Fourth goes to Paramount’s third frame of Johnny Depp Christmas movie, Ebenezer with $1.5M today at 3,180 sites and a 3-day between $6.8M-$7.3M, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s fourth frame of I Play Rocky at 2,711 with $1.4M today, 3-day of $6.6M, and 5-day of $9.5M for a running cume of $22.5M.

Outside the top 5 is Netflix’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 251 locations with $1M today, $3M 3-day and 5-day of $5M.

WEDNESDAY AM: As we told you last night, Lionsgate scored its best Tuesday ever at the domestic box office with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and the best ever for the Suzanne Collins franchise as the day raked in $15.98M.

Recent findings suggest that 2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire owned the previous best Tuesday for the franchise with $15.96M. Running cume for the fifth Francis Lawrence movie is $148.1M and by Thanksgiving, Sunrise on the Reaping will surpass its previous 2023 chapter’s lifetime domestic B.O. of $166.3M.

As we told you, Sunrise on the Reaping will dominate the Thanksgiving Wednesday through Sunday stretch as the franchise has historically done before since 2013, this time with a floor of $70M+. Previously, the pics over Thanksgiving cooked up the following: Catching Fire ($109.9M), Mockingjay Part 1 ($82.6M), Mockingjay Part 2 ($75.9M) with Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes way behind ($42.2M).

According to recent reports, lionsgate has had back-to-back global hit openings this year with Sunrise on the Reaping last weekend at $226.1M WW and Michael with $218.8M. This has all happened under the administration and watch of Motion Picture Chairman, Adam Fogelson. Still no word out there whether or not Lionsgate rejected or accepted Legendary’s bid.

Walt Disney Animation’s Hexed came in with $2.1M, $100K above the $2M we were spotting yesterday. That preview figure is higher than Encanto ($1.5M previews, 5-day of $40.5M) and Wish ($1.8M previews including $500K Saturday sneaks; 5-day of $31.6M). No RT audience score yet, but critics were meh at 67% fresh. There is a chance that the traditional Disney pic comes in lower than its 5-day forecast of $40M-$45M as original animated titles are very challenging to launch in the streaming era, but you have to start some place.

Universal and Paramount’s Focker In-Law, which didn’t have previews last night, rather began showtimes at midnight, has more potential to hit its 5-day forecast of $45M given the Ariana Grande factor and the fact that audiences love the franchise. The first Meet the Parents 26 years ago was the fave among critics at 85% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Focker-in-Law isn’t the worst at 26%, as that belongs to 2010’s Little Fockers. 2004’s Meet the Fockers stands at 39%.

Hexed, Focker-in-Law and Sunrise on the Reaping are sharing PLFs with the latter having Imax screens (except for AMC where they are being designated to Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth).

Thank God for Lionsgate Hunger Games at the box office: Sans a Wicked, Moana and a Zootopia, the Thanksgiving box office will certainly be down from last year’s five day robust $290.3M, which was the fifth best ever. Moana 2 and Wicked led the holiday to its best haul ever with $424.9M.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Samsung S90H OLED TV is a winning 2026 release from Samsung, delivering impressively vibrant yet natural colors and striking contrast. An upgraded version of the S90F, with better glare protection and brighter SDR brightness, it has been praised as one of the most versatile OLED TVs, especially for daytime viewing. Right now, a 55-inch Samsung S90H OLED TV is $400 off on Amazon at a record low of $1,197.99 (originally $1,597.99) for Black Friday. It’s worth noting that the other sizes are also discounted, with the 77-inch model 29% off.

It has been revealed that while it has identical pixel-level contrast and wide viewing angles compared to the S90F, the major upgrade here is a matte-like screen, previously only seen on Samsung’s pricier models like the S95 series, bringing an extra perk and better reflection control for those with sunny media rooms. Contrast and color accuracy are highlights on this model, as is shadow detail.

The S90H offers four HDMI 2.1 inputs and supports refresh rates up to 165Hz with a compatible PC, up from the S90F’s 144Hz. It also supports VRR, FreeSync Premium Pro, G-SYNC, and ALLM. Like its predecessor, it’s powered by the NQ4 AI Gen3 processor for picture and audio processing. Its 40W, 2.1-channel speaker system supports Dolby Atmos, although neither TV supports Dolby Vision.

If you’re looking for a well-equipped OLED at a mid-range price, the discounted 55-inch Samsung S90H is worth considering, especially if you’re a PC gamer or watch in a room prone to glare. It offers a stronger feature set than the S85H without requiring the jump to the more expensive S95H. Just compare the S90F’s current price before buying, particularly if movie nights in a dark room are your priority.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wu-Tang Clan showcased a slew of classic hits during the NFL Thanksgiving Day Game Halftime Show.

The annual match-up pitted the Chicago Bears against the Detroit Lions at at Ford Field in Detroit, with the hip-hop group taking the field midway through. The game, which aired on CBS, also saw Broadway singer Antonio Cipriano performing the National Anthem.

It has been revealed that the group, joined by Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith on drums, kicked it off with “Triumph” from their 1997 album Wu-Tang Forever. The rappers also showcased a medley that included “C.R.E.A.M,” “Da Mystery of Chessboxin,” and “Bring Da Ruckus.” Notably, Ol’ Dirty Bastard’s son Young Dirty Bastard performed his father’s lines off 1995 single “Shimmy Shimmy Ya.”.

Industry observers note that wu-Tang Clan were recently inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame during a ceremony in Los Angeles. During the ceremony, all living members of the Staten Island group hit the stage to perform a medley of some of their biggest hits, including “C.R.E.A.M.” and “Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nuthing ta F’ Wit.” They got a spirited introduction from Chris Rock. Earlier this year, the group celebrated the Knicks’ championship victory with a performance on The Tonight Show. The musicians showcased a medley of performed a medley of two songs, “Bring Da Ruckus” and “C.R.E.A.M.,” on the late-night show, with the help of the NBA team themselves.

Sources indicate that wu-Tang Clan played a small (but apocryphally pivotal) role in the team’s championship run. During Game Four, the Wu-Tang Clan provided the halftime entertainment, taking the stage when the Knicks were down a seemingly insurmountable 29 points. Had the Knicks lost, the Spurs would’ve tied the series at two games apiece. Despite the heavy deficit, Method Man ended the performance by declaring, “Knicks in five.” The team then rallied to win Game Four 107 – 106, then dispatched the Spurs in Game Five a couple of days later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents ….

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:.

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce newly introduced ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve notable actions. The organization has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a newly introduced blog post, Meta says:.

It has been revealed that muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

The best streaming devices are a relatively cheap way to upgrade your TV's streaming capabilities. If you have a non-smart TV, these HDMI-attached dongles and boxes mean you can use it to stream from all your favorite apps. But they're also a good option if you have a great TV with older software.

For most people, the best streaming device is the Roku Streaming Stick Plus. It has an app store, easy access to all your services and won't break the bank. If you're after a more polished experience (especially if you own an iPhone), then the Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is your best bet, but it'll set you back a lot.

These two are not your only options, though. We've tested the best streaming devices available right now, including options from Amazon and Google, to help you upgrade your home viewing experience without breaking the bank, and saving you from needing to replace a perfectly good TV just to get upcoming software.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Roku's streaming devices have topped this list for a long time, and the latest Roku Streaming Stick Plus is only going to cement the brand's place at the top of the tree. The Streaming Stick Plus has loads of features that make it the best option around right now, from fantastic 4K streaming to a simple, slick UI.

Industry observers note that this compact wonder brings powerful streaming without taking up loads of room behind your TV. Roku's user interface is among the best around, making searching through your favorite streaming services a breeze. The Roku remote that comes with it isn't the fanciest, but it's well laid out and simple to use, and supports voice commands.

The most crucial part, of course, is how good it makes your TV shows look. And, despite its lower price, we're happy to report that the 4K output is excellent. We combined it with a Samsung OLED TV, and it looked about as spectacular as you might expect.

It has been revealed that roku has slipped in some funky extras as well. We really like the screensavers — called Backdrops — that play when you're not using the TV. It avoids image retention and burn-in, which is a bonus, but it also makes what could be a big, black rectangle in your room something that actually adds to the decor.

The biggest drawback is the pesky ads. Make sure you turn off video autoplay, lest you be bombarded by irritating, noisy videos on startup. The ads are otherwise relatively easy to ignore. Despite the annoying ads, the Roku Streaming Stick Plus is an excellent streamer.

Sources indicate that it's forty bucks. That's the pitch. It's just about the cheapest way to make your aging TV into a streaming powerhouse. There are fewer bells and whistles, and it doesn't have the highest resolution, but it doesn't cost much and means you can watch Amazon Prime, Netflix and more on your TV.

There are more features than you'd expect, though. While you won't get 4K, you do get some more premium sound formats like Dolby Atmos, should you be hooked up to a surround sound system. There are HDR formats galore as well, so the 1080p image will be super clear and colorful.

In a recent development, it's easy to set up and works speedily with the included remote control. It's not fancy, but it's cheap. And if you want to get the cheapest and easiest way to get streaming, there's not much better. Just don't bother if your TV is a smart TV — the built-in streaming is better.

The Google TV Streamer is a huge improvement over the old Google Chromecast. Similar functionality and navigation remain — and now you get live TV integration, tons of free content, plus several live TV services to choose from (YouTube TV, Sling and Philo).

Industry observers note that but now, it also packs 4K UHD streaming with support for HDR and Dolby Vision for excellent picture quality, and Dolby Atmos for immersive sound. And with Google TV, you have support for over 6,500 Android TV apps.

That's not all, as the TV Streamer has a slew of smart home integrations that make it stand out. Directly from your TV, you can now monitor and control all your smart home devices.

We were able to view live streams from our various home security cameras and video doorbells, and also see which lights were still on — and dim them, too. You can even check the temperature on your smart thermostat. It's a step up from what other streaming devices offer and will make smart home enthusiasts gush the world over.

As with most newer TV models, Google has also incorporated its Gemini AI into the TV Streamer. This will do a variety of tasks, like providing simple summaries of whatever content is on-screen and pulling in reviews from both critics and the general public — for better or worse.

You can also use Gemini to create screensavers. Think of (almost) anything and speak it into the remote, and Gemini will create it for you, to amusing (or horrifying) effect.

Industry observers note that one of the most surprising things about the 2026 Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is not that it now comes with AI, but that it is twice the price of the 2022 version. That's an incredible jump in cost, even considering the price hikes we've seen across all areas of our lives. Whether it's justified depends on how much you use Apple's services.

In a recent development, taking price out for a moment, the experience of using the Apple TV 4K is fantastic. It's uncluttered and easily links up to your non-Apple streaming apps like Netflix. Of course, one of the main attractions is how seamlessly it integrates with Apple's services and hardware, which is why it's the best streaming device for iPhone owners too.

Which brings us back to the price. Unless you have an iPhone or heavily use the Apple TV streaming service, it's probably not worth the investment. But the quality-of-life features you get with an iPhone make the price easier to swallow. Some of the smallest features on tvOS (Apple's software) are actually the best.

In a recent development, the included Siri remote uses an iPod-like touch scroller, which is great for navigation but pretty useless for text entry. So when you tap a text box, an Apple TV keyboard pops up on your iPhone, so you can easily enter usernames and passwords. But in theory, the biggest addition to the 2026 model is Siri's Apple Intelligence upgrade.

It has been revealed that it's not hugely exciting, but it is a step up from Classic Siri. We tried Classic and AI Siri voice commands, asking for lists of movies with certain actors. Classic wouldn't get it right, but AI-powered Siri did just what we asked. It's good, not great, and depending on your views on AI, might not be worth twice the price of the 2022 edition.

Industry observers note that we test streaming players by looking at both the content they can provide (most are very similar at this point) and how they deliver said content. Any streaming player worth its salt can load a 4K stream, but only a good one possesses straightforward navigation, robust search features and a wide variety of content to suit all tastes.

Industry observers note that the first thing we evaluate is the setup, to see how quick and simple it is. From there, we take the user interface for a spin to see what content gets highlighted, what gets hidden, and how easy it is to navigate to our favorite channels.

As live TV service integration becomes a bigger feature in streaming devices, we look at how these sticks and boxes can place your favorites within closer reach.

We'll also watch a few different demonstrates on a variety of channels to gauge the quality of the video and audio, to make sure they look good regardless of whether you have one of the best TVs or not.

After that, it's onto the extra features, like gaming, voice search and screen mirroring. These factors don't weigh quite as heavily toward the final score, but they're nice to have if they work well, and extremely distracting if they don't.

The main reason to get a streaming stick is that your TV is either missing a feature you want, or you'd rather not replace a perfectly good television just because it doesn't connect to the internet and download apps.

These are both great reasons to invest in these small and relatively inexpensive devices. After all, even the best TVs under $500 are still a strain on your bank balance, and if there's nothing wrong with your existing set, why send it out to the trash when you don't need to?

Industry observers note that but if you buy a TV, you'll end up using the software that comes installed on it. With the best streaming devices, you have a lot more choice. Generally speaking, the cheaper devices are supported by ads or feature-locked subscriptions/upgrades. But if you want to get what I'd argue is the best streaming device for iPhone owners (that's the Apple TV 4K), you'll need to spend more, but it's an entirely uncluttered, ad-free experience.

According to recent reports, although for other tech devices, there'd be a lot more between them, the choice here really comes down to price, brand and software. All the devices we've featured have apps for the major streaming platforms, so you won't miss out. Not that I really recommend AI, but the Google TV Streamer is ideal if you're a significant Gemini user.

Or if you want to go the other way, I'd advise the Apple TV 4K — not because it doesn't have AI (the 2026 box has the new AI Siri experience), but because it's not that interesting, so you won't ever feel compelled to use it. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.
  • Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how customers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.
  • Sources indicate that iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how customers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

Sources indicate that iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

It has been revealed that one of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point customers toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

According to recent reports, apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the upcoming Siri experience.

Recent findings suggest that the last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the fresh behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Industry observers note that ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. According to recent reports, iOS 27 brought several latest features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Industry observers note that siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a substantial upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

Industry observers note that in Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Recent findings suggest that since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of owners have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

It has been revealed that thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:.

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’.

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

  • It has been revealed that J oni Mitchell wanted to go ice skating.
  • Recent findings suggest that mitchell had recently cancelled the remainder of her Hissing of Summer Lawns tour, performing her last show at the nearby Dane County Memorial Coliseum.
  • In a recent development, legendary photographer Joel Bernstein captured this moment, which would eventually appear inside the gatefold for her next album: Hejira.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that J oni Mitchell wanted to go ice skating. It was February 1976, and she was standing on the edge of a frozen Lake Mendota in Madison, Wisconsin, wearing a black ermine cape and a black wool hat. All she needed were black skates to match. “I had a hell of a time getting the guy to give me black skates,” she recalled to Cameron Crowe, decades later. “He said, ‘Black skates are for, for men, madam.’ I said, ’No, no, you don’t understand. I’m having a funeral for my dead tour. I need black.”.

Recent findings suggest that mitchell had recently cancelled the remainder of her Hissing of Summer Lawns tour, performing her last show at the nearby Dane County Memorial Coliseum. She was exhausted, battling a cocaine addiction, and reeling from the breakup with her drummer John Guerin, which she’d later describe as “one of the most special relationships” she’d ever had. This was her wake for it all, a farewell ride through the ice — not so different from the “River” she dreamt about skating on just five years prior. The ice was starting to thaw, and there were loud crashing sounds coming from the nearby trees, a sound she likened to “cases of Coca-Cola smashing.” She began to skate anyway, her black outfit standing in stark contrast to the backdrop.

In a recent development, legendary photographer Joel Bernstein captured this moment, which would eventually appear inside the gatefold for her next album: Hejira. On the front cover, taken by Norman Seef, she’s wearing a black beret and holding a cigarette, stoically staring at the camera (she wanted it to look like an Ingmar Bergman film, she stated), as a wide, open road is juxtaposed below. The artwork indicated the mission statement of Hejira — in the same way she skated away on that ice and didn’t look back, Mitchell got in her car and drove. “The Hejira album was written mostly while I was traveling in the car,” she told Crowe, in her 1979 Rolling Stone cover story. “That’s why there were no piano songs, if you remember. Hejira was an obscure word, but it said exactly what I wanted. Running away, honorably.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Recent findings suggest that mitchell took three journeys while making Hejira: a portion of Bob Dylan’s all-star Rolling Thunder Revue Tour in late 1975, her short-lived Hissing trek in early 1976, and a cross-country drive she made in a white Mercedes without a license (she’d often wear a red wig in disguise, and go by names like Charlene Latimer and Joan Black). Released in November 1976, the album is a timeless travelogue of jazz-folk magic, when Mitchell left it all behind in search for more. “I’m porous with travel fever,” she sings on the aching title track. “But you know I’m so glad to be on my own.”.

It’s impossible to pinpoint the genius of Hejira on just one track. There’s the opener “Coyote,” about the affair she had with the playwright Sam Shephard on the Rolling Thunder tour. That song is now immortalized in a viral video from Martin Scorsese’s documentary, where she casually performs it for a stunned Dylan, Roger McGuinn, and Gordon Lightfoot. There’s “Furry Sings the Blues,” about her encounter with the Memphis blues legend who didn’t exactly take a liking to her (yes, that’s her longtime pal Neil Young on the harmonica). The stunning “Amelia,” named after Amelia Earhart, was her ode “from one solo pilot to another …sort of reflecting on the cost of being a woman and having something you must do.” Hejira is arguably her most cohesive body of work, featuring the fretless bass of Jaco Pastorius — whom she called the bass player of her dreams — plus guitarist Larry Carlton, percussionist Bobbye Hall, and others.

Looking back, Mitchell knew she was at the height of her powers. “I feel a lot of people could have written ’Chelsea Morning,’” she said. “But I don’t think anyone else could have written the songs on Hejira.” In honor of the 50th anniversary of Hejira, Rolling Stone spoke with musicians and actors about its legacy, and why it continues to resonate with listeners today. And in a full-circle moment, Crowe, who is at the moment working on a Mitchell biopic, pays tribute to the record he discussed with Mitchell in this very magazine, all those years ago. I’ve been a Joni Mitchell fan for a really long time, since I was a kid. And one of my best friends who passed away, we were obsessed with her. She was the one who actually introduced me to Joni Mitchell through Blue, because we would just listen to the album all the time. So through a general obsession with her, I just eventually went through all of her albums. And I really remember being particularly attached to Hejira when I was a teenager. I would go on long walks around my neighborhood [in Oak Park in Illinois], listening to that album, and just be really emotional.

Jaco’s bass literally captures the feeling of being on a trip and moving. He uses his bass as a vehicle on that album in such a cool way. And Joni’s lyrics feel like being on a road trip, listening to somebody’s stories. It reminds me of being with my parents, driving. We always drive from Chicago to Georgia where my family’s from, and just being on the road and talking.

The album itself feels like a departure. She’s going on a journey and choosing to go away from the industry for a minute, and that is captured sonically in a really interesting way. With Hejira, she distills the feeling of loneliness in a way that she hadn’t done before. Each song is dealing with loneliness, but she puts it into these different scenarios and narratives. They all come together to tell this one story of being a woman who’s alone, just traveling.

In Martin Scorsese’s film The Rolling Thunder Review: A Bob Dylan Story, there is a moment where Joni plays her new song, “Coyote,” at Gordon Lightfoot’s house. I love that there is footage of the early creation of this song. The lyrics change a little on the album, but you can see in her eyes the memories are very powerful as she sings and remembers. She had just written “Coyote” on a bus when she was with the tour, as she looked out at the “white lines on the freeway,” after she had a brief, tumultuous affair with the playwright Sam Shepard. Most of us have had these youthful, quick assignations, and I love being in her head as she reconciles the moment through her poetry and lyricism. Hejira is filled with emotion and hunger and as a young woman. Hejira helped me with the complexities of life, love, and longing.

It’s something that stayed with me my whole life. Being somebody who makes records and always having trouble listening to records because you’re just always thinking about technically how they were made, it’s a beautiful example of just being so disconnected from any kind of process. It doesn’t bear examination. I just find it 100 percent an emotional reactive experience. It conjures up something that I am so desperate to hold onto in my life. Basically what I’m saying is, I’m just a sad, pathetic fan, really.

Sources indicate that those things get chipped away gradually, as you meet all your heroes and make a lot of music. You never really listen to music the same way. But I’m a teenager again when I listen to it. I don’t know if it’s the imagery or the fact that she has this incredible way of weaving a narrative that is just so difficult to do in song. I mean, poetry is powerful, but the combination of melody and poetry is this kind of witchcraft that has always cast a spell on me.

In a recent development, she’s my favorite artist. And this record is an apex of confidence. She’s really just doing what she wants, to the nth degree. She’s this crazy sort of enigmatic, weird figure. You hear all these stories about her. She’s a manifestation of something that is so rare and special that my version of her that I have in my heart and my idea of who she is, I’m just clinging onto it for dear life. It’s like a hero I never want to meet. She could be the nicest, warmest person on Earth, but she wouldn’t be this person that she’s created in my mind personally, by my personal relationship with her music.

I remember hearing a long time ago that Joni wrote most of Hejira while she was on a road trip across America, and ever since then, I’ve always listened to it on long drives. It just makes so much sense to me. The whole record feels like it’s constantly moving, whether you’re speeding down a highway or sitting in traffic watching the sun go down.

As a drummer first, I’m always listening for the drums and percussion on records. To me, they’re kind of the heartbeat of any modern album. I know a lot of Joni’s records don’t have much drumming on them, but the fact that Hejira is constantly chugging along without a lot of full kit drumming continues to blow my mind. And I think Jaco’s bass playing adds this whole other rhythmic dimension to her music.

I’ve always thought of Joni as a percussionist in her own way. The way she attacks the guitar strings, the rhythms she creates with her strumming, it’s unlike anything I’ve ever heard from another musician. It’s one of the most fascinating things about her playing to me. And then you have Jaco on bass, another absolute master of rhythm, and the two of them create this incredible, almost hypnotic pulse that runs through the whole record.

And Bobbye Hall’s percussion adds so much to that feeling. It’s never overpowering, but there’s so much movement and texture in what she’s doing. All these little rhythmic details that somehow make the music feel even more alive. Between the three of them, there’s this constant sense of motion, like the music is always pushing forward but never in a hurry to get anywhere.

It has been revealed that hejira was the Joni album that helped me meet Joni. I feel like her truest self comes through on this record so beautifully, and it’s an anchor on tour when the roads are never ending and the bus forever rumbling. My favorite song is “Coyote.”.

According to recent reports, hejira is Joni’s culmination to my mind. Her greatest songs, the greatest band, the greatest recordings, the most revelatory. The signature Roland Jazz Chorus guitar amp tone. Jaco Pastorius truly unleashed. The concepts and material mined into their seventh and eighth minute in some cases. I like to believe her whole catalog was leading to this moment. She’s at the height of her powers, and the masterworks that follow (Don Juan’s Reckless Daughter, Mingus, Night Ride Home, Turbulent Indigo, etc.) feel possible because of what Hejira unlocked. The writing is perhaps the most challenging, but the experience remains incredibly propulsive; you’re carried along by bearing witness to a human truly unrestrained by self-doubt, by adhering to any kind of rules or any kind of culture, someone in the midst of their quest to express their purest self. Maybe that sounds vague, but anyone that knows the record knows exactly what I’m talking about. When I’ve been asked about it, I’ve jokingly replied, “It’s as far as music has come.” But maybe that’s actually true.

It has been revealed that I was touring extensively through my twenties, and I think it was at least 10 months of the year I was just on the road constantly. It was such a grind, but music had become a companion. We all had our headphones, and you’d sit on these long plane rides and bus rides listening to records. So it’s a lot of time to take a lot of deep dives. The whole Odelay tour, I was listening to Joni on the bus. It was pretty much Joni, Françoise Hardy records from the mid Sixties, and Morricone soundtracks — but not the Westerns, the weirder stuff. And then I had a CD of a rainstorm in Hawaii. That was all I listened to. It was like Joni and a Hawaiian rainstorm.

Industry observers note that hejira is the sound of an artist who has evolved so deeply into their own voice and their own craft. It’s a thing to behold. It’s a place that not a lot of artists even get to. Either they’re not really on that search to cultivate that rarefied place in their work, or they’re distracted by success and fame and touring, which happens to anybody who gets caught up in the sort of mechanics of the music business. So I think it’s even more of a singular achievement that she was able to make this after being on such a nonstop, relentless decade of making albums and touring. Usually at that point, somebody would just want to disappear for five years.

The music doesn’t necessarily sound like anything she had done before. One thing that’s really striking to me is the guitar sound. The effect on her guitar is a chorus pedal. The first one came out the year she was making the record. This was brand upcoming technology. So this is like, “This new weird thing came out, and I’m going to put it on my entire album.” Not even, “Let’s vet this and see if this is cool. Is this going to be trendy? Is this going to sound dated?” This chorus pedal becomes the sound of whole genres afterwards. I don’t think it really becomes part of the palette of popular music till maybe the early 2010s. You listen to almost all of indie rock, from Mac DeMarco, to pop artists.

And then you also get the guitar sound of Prince’s Purple Rain, which comes from this record, without a doubt. It is interesting that something that is uncompromising, and not even her most popular album or most iconic, still managed to have an imprint on pop. Honestly, I think the sound of this even filters into shoegaze and Cocteau Twins. I don’t know if people have put those things together, but I see it clearly.

It has been revealed that she is so mature as an artist on this record. I mean, it would take you more than a lifetime to get to that maturity. Somehow, she did it.

I first listened to Hejira in full on a tour bus driving through Europe. Highway rushing past, barren fields and long stretches of countryside out the window, the way Joni intended (I think). It struck me immediately as a timeless record. None of the songs are shorter than four minutes, the longest one being almost nine, but somehow they all feel intentional. She doesn’t waste words. I was so intrigued by that concept, of letting the story speak for itself, and setting up a bed of guitars that could support it. It inspired my writing a lot during that time, specifically a song I wrote while on that tour called “Our Strange Ways.” This record feels hypnotic and deeply meditative. And listening to it as I felt, quite literally, like a prisoner of the white lines on the freeway, was an experience I will never forget. One of my top Joni records of all time.

Sources indicate that long country drives are still my favorite way to pass the time, and Hejira captures why better than any other record I’ve heard. There was a year maybe where I’d point the car in some direction and only play Hejira, on a loop, until I’d memorized every melodic variation and phrase, as if getting a handle on the twists and turns of those infinite songs would give me a better handle on the twists and turns of life itself. I love the interior drama, the humor, the mise en scène, the acceptance of uncertainty and change. The chords, the tunings, obviously. My dad idolized Jaco growing up and makes his own fretless basses, so I hear my dad playing with Joni on the Jaco songs.

Once when I was making lectures for a songwriting class I was undeservingly teaching, I tried writing one about, forgive me, the “multi-perspectival sublime.” I wanted to relate Hejira to the painting “Las Meninas” by Velázquez and how, the longer you look at both, the harder it is to make sense of you-the-viewer’s place in it. Looking at “Las Meninas,” at first the viewer feels that everyone in the painting is looking baldly at them, but as you look closer, you realize the “viewer” is in an impossible position, and likely isn’t in the room at all. The songs on Hejira do this for me. They seem to be about the self, but the perspective shifts rapidly, from a man and a woman sitting on a rock to a blue motel room to a marble bowling ball, from a roadside gas station to the cosmos, a chimney becomes a flag reflected from a bank window into a hotel room — the center is always shifting, to such a degree that the viewer loses their sense of self and surrenders to liminality in a sort of holy way.

I didn’t finish the essay because it’s hard to write about a feeling like that without reducing it to platitudes, and I’m no Peter Schjeldahl. But Hejira really does help me transcend the self, with its trick mirrors and micro-to-macro shifts and its sense of spiritual surrender and leggerezza. It’s my deepest musical attachment, no question.

According to recent reports, god, this record. I had a dream once where Joni was sitting on a dock on a lake in Canada singing “Coyote,” with all my family in the water, singing along in the sun. Needless to say, this record and Joni’s voice has been extremely influential to me, even making its way into my dreams!

It has been revealed that the freedom in this record, the six-, seven-, eight-minute long songs, her storytelling, taking you on the long and winding road with her. She always reminds me there are no rules. I think my favorite song is “Amelia”: “It was the hexagram of the heavens/It was the strings of my guitar.” She is the master. I am so grateful to have been introduced to Joni so young, her voice as a North Star.

According to recent reports, something I love and admire about Joni is that she never made the same record twice, even though she easily could have, considering how strong her lyrics are on their own. I love the way Joni uses the electric guitar on Hejira. To me, it sounds like rain running down the window of a moving car, which feels so fitting when you think of the record as a kind of travel diary.

According to recent reports, I remember the first time I heard “Amelia.” I kept thinking, how does she write a song about someone or something so far removed from my own life, and yet make me see so much of myself in it? Or the way she uses the Cold War as a metaphor in “Blue Motel Room.” That’s what Joni’s lyrics do. They hold a mirror up to whoever is listening without ever seeming to try too hard. Something I often ask myself when I’m writing, especially when listening to a song like “Blue Motel Room,” is how to bring the wider world into the microcosm of everyday life. How do you take something so vast and make it feel so intimate? Joni does that beautifully, and I think it really shines through on Hejira.

In a recent development, joni Mitchell is one of those songwriters that I go to whenever I have writer’s block — she always provides a well of inspiration. My song “Keep You” is a direct homage to “Coyote” that evoked a scandalous song about love through a free spirit. Lines like “you’ll be brushing out a brood mare’s tail” were scrubbed into imagery like “brushing out the mane of a silver healer.” I love to pull from Joni’s work. She is a huge inspiration to me.

In a recent development, I don’t even know where to begin with Hejira, because it has touched my life in so many profound ways. At first, when I was little and just old enough to hum along to the melodies. Again, when I was a few years older and learning how to play “Coyote” on the guitar. And then a few years later, when I started reading the lyrics of songs I liked and being inspired to start writing my own, which led to my career in songwriting. I remember driving from Maine to L.A. in pursuit of my dream, during which I, of course, listened to Hejira, because I felt as though I was living every lyric in real time. Now as a 34-year-old woman, I continue to return to it as if it’s a friend going through all the same growing pains I’m going through — constantly in search of something, and simultaneously asking if the major dream is worth the loneliness that often comes with it. Even though it’s nearly impossible to choose a favorite song from the record because they are all so intertwined to me, if I had to pick, I’d say “Amelia.” Everything about it. The chord changes. The guitar tones. And of course the perfectly poetic yet heart-wrenchingly clear lyrics that describe two women choosing ambition, exploration, and the unknown. I’m forever grateful to Joni for this album, and my life would be drastically different without it.

Hejira lives in its own world, a sonic-travelogue written on Mitchell’s 1976 journey across America. It’s her most cinematic album too, filled with restless wonder and the characters she’d met along the way. The album was born out of the end of Mitchell’s relationship with drummer John Guerin. They’d lived and toured together. “We had a hard time letting each other go,” says Mitchell today. Her popularity was at a peak after Court and Spark, but a tour of America’s arenas left her missing the intimacy and sound of smaller venues and clubs. She cancelled an upcoming European tour, went skating on Madison, Wisconsin’s icy Lake Mendota (the “bird in flight” series was memorably captured by photographer Joel Bernstein) and headed back to California with the notion that it was time to travel, soak up life, seek upcoming inspiration, and find a course-correction before she became “another scribe writing about the life of a rock singer, a minority experience to be sure.”.

In a recent development, life soon arrived with an invitation. Mitchell’s old friend from Toronto, Australian race-champion Vic Wilson, visited Mitchell with his flight-attendant friend Steven. Wilson was looking to borrow a car for a road-trip to Damariscotta, Maine, where he planned to collect his daughter, Larissa, and return to Australia. Mitchell not only loaned them the Bluebird, her white Mercedes coupe, but enthusiastically joined them with guitar, a suitcase, and sketchpads. (Her car would soon break down and need to be replaced on the road.) It has been revealed that parting company with her road-trip buddies in Newly introduced York city, Mitchell rode back alone. It was America’s Bicentennial summer. With roadmaps (and no driver’s license), she worked her way down the East Coast, through Charleston, South Carolina, the pageantry of small town parades, pinball buddies, flag-draped cafes. Though the disguise rarely escaped close examination, Mitchell often wore a red wig and traveled by the name Charlene Latimer. At night she collected the thoughts of the day and wrote songs filled with longing and delight and raw introspection. “I knew it was a growth step for me,” she reflects today, listening to “Song For Sharon” and other songs from the album. She adds one small disappointment. Nearly back home from her solo return, Mitchell stopped to join Bob Dylan’s Rolling Thunder revue for a show in Ft. Worth. Her artist’s portfolio containing all the Hejira drawings were stolen from her hotel room.

The songs remain. Each one is filled with memory and detail and stunning reflection, but don’t forget to listen to Hejira as a whole. There’s a movie in every full-listen. To further appreciate Hejira, it’s also fun to consider what popular music sounded like in the summer of 1976. It was the peak of disco, radio was filled with the Bee Gees, the thump-thump-thump of post-Saturday Night Fever. Heard in context today, especially with the bass explorations of Jaco Pastorious, Hejira sounds like music from another planet. For any fan who joined the Joni Mitchell journey with Blue, the elixir of Hejira is the adventure you didn’t expect. Mitchell’s own rules for writing the album: “Summon a melody and some chords, write the words …then ask yourself if you’ve done anything like it before. If you have, start over.”.

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-fresh iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

According to recent reports, the iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

Sources indicate that the iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

According to recent reports, for most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

Industry observers note that the iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

It has been revealed that still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

#131383. We've tested the best smartwatches, and these are the 3 I recommend for iPhone and Android
