We've tested the best smartwatches, and these are the 3 I recommend for iPhone and Android

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone.
  • Industry observers note that one of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which debuted the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android.
  • It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone. Over the past few years, brands have moved away from universal compatibility and toward platform-specific watches that will only work if you use a particular phone.

Industry observers note that one of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which debuted the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android. It's half the price of Apple or Google's watches, but you wouldn't know it from its impressive fitness tracking features.

It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Amazfit Active 3 Premium is the smartwatch I recommend for most people, and not just because it works with whichever phone you have. It's a fantastic fitness-tracking watch that easily holds its own against the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5, without locking you to a specific platform or phone.

Recent findings suggest that it is also incredible value — coming in at around half the price of the two flagship watches — and all the features are free with no subscription (unless you need Zepp Aura, the sleep-focused AI wellness app that generates audio to relax you). It has offline maps, tracks more than 170 activities, and comes with built-in GPS.

Recent findings suggest that it has a smaller footprint (wristprint?) than many other smartwatches, with a 1.3-inch display, compared to the 1.77- or 1.96-inch Apple Watch Series 12. It's not a huge amount on paper, but it makes a big difference, as it felt smaller and less noticeable on our wrist. It's a shame it doesn't come in a few more vibrant colors, though.

While you don't get the smarts of Apple and Google's watches (emergency alerts, on-watch calls, third-party apps), fitness and activity tracking is where the Active 3 Premium really shines, with metrics to rival the best Garmin watches, like heart rate, blood oxygen, stress levels, cycle tracking, sleep quality and skin temperature.

The data all syncs to your phone, and you can view it and get insights in the Zepp app, available for Android and iPhone. If you ever used a Fitbit before the Google takeover, the Zepp app is the closest thing to that now-gone experience; easy to understand, straightforward to use, and guides you through all the different metrics.

This is particularly helpful if you're just getting into running, as the running features on the Active 3 Premium are almost as detailed as those you'd find on Garmin watches, yet everything is explained clearly, even for more complex topics like your lactate threshold and ground contact time, which assess how your foot strikes the floor.

According to recent reports, amazfit claims that the Active 3 Premium should last 12 days between charges. Like most other smartwatches, that doesn't work out in the real world; we found that it'd generally last just over a week or eight days. That's down a bit on the spec, but still miles ahead of the 24-hour battery life on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Apple, Google and Samsung refresh their watches every year. Normally, these are pretty small upgrades, so I often recommend buying the previous year's model. But not with the Apple Watch Series 12. For the first time in almost half a decade, Apple has given the watch a pretty big health-tracking patch.

The most significant change is that there's a new, more accurate heart rate sensor. This powers a few other changes, like the Readiness score you can get each day. This is something imported from other running watches and is a measure of how you've recovered after activity and how to improve the score.

Sources indicate that I've tested watches with this kind of score and haven't found it that informative, but I know our resident runners find it particularly helpful when training for races. The improved sensors also allow for continuous heart rate monitoring (ie all day), which was previously limited to just during tracked workouts.

These practical and useful changes were only part of the Series 12 pitch. Apple also rolled out latest AI Siri and a selection of 'helpful' AI-powered features, called Audio Intelligence. There are two (Live Rewind, Siri Recap), but both use the watch to capture speech around you and turn it into some form of recap.

In a recent development, live Rewind is arguably the least helpful and most invasive. It listens to conversations (privately on your phone) and allows you to rewind live conversations in case you miss a detail, like someone's name (in case you were unaware you could ask the person to repeat what they said). Recap uses AI to summarize all that data into a journal-like, 'here's what happened today' note.

In a recent development, honestly, these seem like gimmicks to me that very few people will ever use, and it normalizes surveillance. So, in case it wasn't clear, I wouldn't buy the watch for these and would jump into the settings to disable them. But in all other aspects, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch you can buy right now and a worthy upgrade.

As with the Apple Watch, I wouldn't normally recommend the most recent version of the Google Pixel Watch, but this time I do think the Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better choice than the 4, but mostly because it's hard to find a newly introduced edition of the Pixel Watch 4 now that the Pixel Watch 5 exists.

In a recent development, that doesn't mean I don't think the Pixel Watch 5 is a great smartwatch — it is — but it's a relatively modest patch this time around. But what you get for your money still makes it the best smartwatch for Android phones, especially if you own a Pixel device. And like Apple, it's the new health and safety features that are the headline.

Recent findings suggest that the Pixel Watch 5 includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is a lot like 2024's Loss of Pulse Detection, which uses the watch's sensor data to look for signs of a breathing emergency and automatically requests 911 support or trusted contacts for help. These two, along with Fall/Crash Detection, Blood Pressure Trends, and Insulin Resistance Trends, form part of Google's upcoming "Health Guardian" suite.

Technologically, it's impressive. But do I recommend you buy the watch for them? I don't think so. It's a reassuring fallback if you do have an emergency, but you can't say with certainty that they'll always work as intended when you need them to. And reviewers (including us) can't really test them to check either.

Sources indicate that what I like about the Pixel Watch range is that Google doesn't tie too many features exclusively to Pixel phones. The Pixel-exclusive features on the Watch 5 are: call screening, secure phone unlock, contact cards when someone calls you, and the ability to use your watch as a remote viewfinder for your phone's camera app.

It has been revealed that the newest watch has also retained my favorite feature: repairable screens and replaceable batteries. This isn't as easy as popping the back off, but it makes the Pixel Watch 5 the most repairable smartwatch you can buy right now. iFixit even rated it a near-perfect 9/10 for repairability, while the Apple Watch Series 12 scored just 4/10.

It has been revealed that it's not easy for me to praise Google (have you seen the Google Graveyard?), but it's a hugely positive move that saves you money in the long run and prevents otherwise good watches from going to the trash. But much of this was also true of the Pixel Watch 4, so if you can find a good deal on the older model, I'd go for that.

Sources indicate that if you're after the best smartwatch for your phone, the three models I recommend above are going to cover most use cases, whichever phone you have. But there are a lot more smartwatches around right now.

Industry observers note that not every model can be the best, but some come pretty close. If you need a few more options, these are the smartwatches I still think are worth your money, and may fill a need we didn't cover in the wearables from Amazfit, Apple or Google.

It has been revealed that last year's Apple Watch Series 11 is so close to the older Series 10 that it does make you wonder why Apple released it, but for the first time in many years, there was a bump in battery life from 18 hours on the Series 10 to 24 hours on the Series 11. If you can get a good discount, it's a great option, but the Series 12 is a much better watch for not much more.

Read our full Apple Watch Series 11 review.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 generates free wellbeing insights from your data. This is a neat upside, as many other brands charge for this. The (potential) downside is that you need a Samsung phone to access them all in the Samsung Health app. But it's more expensive than the Galaxy Watch 8, despite modest changes and the same display. The Pixel Watch 5 is a better option unless you really need the Samsung integration.

Read our full Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 review.

In a recent development, apple didn't release a newly introduced budget watch in 2026, so the most recent is the 2025 SE 3. It's an excellent choice and has almost all the same features as the Series 10 and 11, minus some health-specific ones like ECG and blood oxygen monitoring. And like those models, it lacks the upgraded health sensors of the Series 12. If you can do without them, the SE 3 is a great value Apple Watch.

Read our full Apple Watch SE 3 review.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a useful upgrade from the Ultra 3 with a redesigned, more accurate health sensor array and better battery life. It also comes with the same AI gimmicks as the Series 12. It's a good option if you need a larger, longer-lasting Apple Watch, but for most people, the Series 12 is the better (and cheaper) choice.

Read our full Apple Ultra 4 review.

The Withings ScanWatch Light is a stripped-back version of the hybrid ScanWatch 2 I wear every day. It doesn't have a large color screen and is missing features like calls and apps, but it can track your activity, heart rate and workouts. I love the ScanWatch 2, and the compromise to reduce the cost is that the Light drops the flagship watch's health features, like an ECG. Otherwise, this is an excellent fitness tracking watch that'll last several weeks between charges.

Read our full Withings ScanWatch Light review.

Sources indicate that the CMF Watch 3 Pro is impressively cheap, retailing for less than most fitness trackers. It has a color display and two weeks of battery life; incredible at this price. But we found that step counts are inaccurate and the sleep tracking is unreliable. So I'd recommend the Amazfit Active 3 Premium instead.

Read our full Nothing CMF Watch 3 Pro review.

We reviewed the first Apple Watch more than a decade ago, and we've been testing the best smartwatches ever since. The devices have gotten more complex, last longer and have way more features now, but the core of our testing has remained the same: we wear the watches, just as you would, to see how they hold up in the real world.

In a recent development, we look at how easy it is to set up, whether it has compatibility challenges with specific phones and spending hours poking around in the software, looking for settings, apps and other features that make the device worth your money. Over the years, these watches have transitioned from phone companions to health and wellbeing trackers.

Recent findings suggest that so we also focus on how these tools work, whether the tracking is accurate, how it compares to the competition and whether there's value in measuring what the tech giant states you should. We wear the best smartwatches out on runs, during workouts, while sleeping and going about our day to see how they cope.

According to recent reports, over the past few years, brands have added more safety features to their watches, like irregular heartbeat notifications, sleep apnea alerts, crash and fall detection and hypertension alerts. These are things we can't practically test, so we can't verify that these work as intended or described.

According to recent reports, in the U.S., health features are regulated by the FDA, so there is some degree of verification, but because we can't check that ourselves, I wouldn't recommend that you buy any of these watches specifically for these safety features. At the very least, they should be secondary to some other safety check.

It's not something you can predict, but sometimes a health problem does come along when you're testing a smartwatch. This happened to one of our writers — her Garmin watch alerted her to a potential heart problem she didn't know about, and that prompted her to go to the hospital to get checked out.

Before you go too far into your journey for a upcoming smartwatch, first you need to work out which ones will work with your phone. The Apple Watch only works with iPhones, and some Android-focused watches have features that are exclusive to specific phones (I'm thinking of offerings from Google and Samsung here).

It has been revealed that there are plenty of options that'll work with both platforms, but they generally aren't the flagship models that get a lot of attention every summer and fall, like the watch I rate as the best smartwatch right now, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium. It's more of a fitness smartwatch, but it can do a lot of what the others can do for a lot less.

In a recent development, and that's one of the other big choices you have to make: do you want a fitness watch that has smartwatch features, or a smartwatch as a companion to your phone that can track your fitness? These sound similar — and they are — but the difference is how much of the focus is put on either the smartwatch or fitness features.

Industry observers note that fitness smartwatches evolved from the best fitness trackers, with larger displays and more sensors. The best smartwatches started life as Bluetooth-connected extensions of your phone and over time became devices that keep you connected to your digital life, even when you're away from your phone working out.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5 are the best compromise between the two, but there are plenty of other options in our Also Consider section that also straddle that line or lean one way or the other. Though, if you need a cellular connection in your watch, those are pretty much limited to the flagship models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

It has been revealed that say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

According to recent reports, the upgrade follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality at the moment on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're at the moment discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

It has been revealed that these headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony claims you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

It has been revealed that personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

CarPlay Ultra first introduced for Aston Martin owners in the United States and Canada. What about other automakers? Here’s what we know.

Industry observers note that 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Sources indicate that in December 2023, Apple said that Porsche and Aston Martin would be the first automakers to support next-generation CarPlay starting in 2024. That deadline came and went, and Apple confirmed in January that next-gen CarPlay had been delayed but was still in development.

Apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The tech giant also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

Industry observers note that when Apple unveiled the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three new partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

It has been revealed that however, several brands have also dropped their looks to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that noted, here is the full list of automakers who blueprint to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of November 2026.

It has been revealed that what do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai confirmed the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major latest Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”.

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

Sources indicate that in a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the tech giant is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:.

In a recent development, “We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”.

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

The question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jack O’Connell is being talked about as a Bond villain, but Danny Boyle states he could have been much more than that.

According to recent reports, boyle, who directed O’Connell in The Sun newspaper movie Ink, was speaking on the Alchemy with Anthony Mason podcast when he made the comment. The conversation turned to the skills of O’Connell and Robert Pattinson, the fresh James Bond, prompting Boyle to discuss the next 007 movie.

“Jack O’Connell would have been a great Bond as well,” he said. “I can see they’re beginning in all this talk they’re talking about Jack O’Connell as a possible villain,” he added, approving of the idea. Related Stories News 'Twilight' Director On Robert Pattinson Landing James Bond Role: "I Almost Fell Out Of My Bed" News 'Daredevil's Charlie Cox Wanted To Audition For James Bond But Was Told He Was "Too Old": "But Robert Pattinson Is The Same Age As Me!".

He added Pattinson and O’Connell had similar screen magnetism. “They have that thing – you want to watch them,” he said. “It’s impossible to quantify what it is, otherwise we’d all buy it for ourselves, but it’s just there and you want to follow them.” Watch on Deadline.

There were some rumors that O’Connell was among those considered for the plum role before Twilight and Dune star Pattinson was selected by Amazon.

As for Pattinson, who beat the likes of Callum Turner and Jack Lowden to become Amazon MGM Studios’ pick for Bond earlier this month, Boyle had nothing but praise.

Industry observers note that “He’s a movie star, and I could see that from the first Twilight films,” he said. “Him and Kristen Stewart, the two of them. You thought: they’re movie stars. It’s a given,” he said. “There’s not that many of them out there, and having a British pedigree will always help him in that world as well.”.

Boyle himself came close to directing 2021 pic No Time to Die, but left the gig after creative differences with producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Last year, he said he had one regret about walking away: His long-time collaborator John Hodge’s script was “really good.”.

Recalling the plan for the film, Boyle said: “We came up with this idea, which was really good. We disagreed about it ultimately, and when you are on those kind of scale of projects, yes you should part company. That’s why the creative differences is such a convenient phrase because if you don’t there will be bloodshed down the line, because there’s so much money at stake. “I think we were all we were all um sanguin about separating.”.

In a recent development, early Black Friday deals are popping up everywhere from Amazon to Costco. For those looking to upgrade an old but smaller TV to a newer model without splurging on an OLED, the 65-inch Samsung M80H Mini-LED TV is 29% off and down to a record-low $497.99 (originally $697.99). If you want to downsize (or go massive), the 55-inch, 75-inch, and 85-inch models are also discounted ahead of the holiday.

According to recent reports, while it’s considered an entry-level 4K smart TV, the M80H is packed with Samsung Vision AI features, and like the rest of the brand’s TVs, it runs on the Tizen interface. A high 144Hz refresh rate, as well as VRR and  AMD FreeSync Premium, makes it a decent choice for gamers compared to the standard 60Hz of cheaper models.

It has been revealed that it has AirPlay support and built-in Alexa, but lacks local dimming and may struggle in very bright, sunlit rooms, so keep that in mind if you do a lot of daytime viewing. That stated, Filmmaker Mode delivers reliable color accuracy for standard dynamic range (SDR) content out of the box. At under $500, the 65-inch Samsung M80H Mini-LED TV is a solid option if you want a big screen and a high refresh rate on a budget.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories.
  • iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways.
  • I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories. Here are my top five picks.

iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways. You’ll now get searchable videos, highlighted clips, 4K support, and more.

I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras. The main difference is video quality, and whether they’re designed for outdoor use or only indoors.

Smart locks have always offered convenience, but with the advent of Ultra Wideband-supported locks, they’re better than ever.

Aqara’s U400 smart lock was among the first to introduce Ultra Wideband, which enables your door to lock and unlock automatically when it senses your presence. Unlike prior smart lock automations that relied on Bluetooth, Ultra Wideband offers excellent reliability and precision for a great overall experience.

According to recent reports, want to open your garage door with a quick Siri command, or via CarPlay or the Home app on iPhone? Smart garage door openers with Apple Home support can deliver that, and my recommendation is the meross MSG150HK.

meross claims the MSG150HK is compatible with “the vast majority of Chamberlain, Lift-Master, and Craftsman brand openers.” And it supports security features like automatic notifications when your door is left open, or every time it opens and closes.

Sources indicate that smart plugs are often a gateway to building out a smart home. And my favorite option, both for cost and convenience, is Tapo’s multipack of smart plugs.

Tapo sells its smart plug in a 2-pack at a great price—currently only $8 per plug. These plugs are compact and offer seamless, quick setup through the Home app without needing a separate app.

Controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually update the thermostat.

Recent findings suggest that what are your top Apple Home accessory recommendations? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that happy Black Friday! While we're not quite at the big day yet, the Black Friday deals are truly here. While I'm often a Black Friday skeptic (as lots of the deals are typically not that great, or worse, misleading), I'm actually quite impressed with the deals on headphones this year.

In a recent development, I'm Pete, reviews editor here at Tom's Guide, and this is my fifth Black Friday working on the site. I'm keeping a close eye on all the best headphones deals.

If you're after a new set of headphones for the gym, the latest waterproof Beats 360 are $100 off at Walmart. The flagship Apple AirPods Max 2 are also reduced from $549 to $419 at Amazon, and the Sony WH-1000XM6 have seen a hefty discount, dropping from $459 to $348 at Amazon.

But there are plenty more deals where those came from.

Sources indicate that soundcore's Q20i have dropped in price for Black Friday. They're comfortable, lightweight and sound great for the price, while also offering ANC.

In a recent development, in our Sony WH-CH530 review, we gave these plucky little cans a full five stars. Why? Because look at that $69 MSRP. That's why. For the money, these cans offer stellar sound, plenty of comfort, solid battery life and fun colorways! And now they're just $38.

Skullcandy literally put a bass slider in these headphones to make them shake on your head. There's a vibration motor in there. So, yeah, if it's bass you're after, and you fancy saving $120, look no further.

Sound, ANC, comfort, styling. These cans have it all. In fact, there was only one thing we didn't like in our Sony WH-CH730N review, and that was the U.S. price of $199 — way higher than the EU and U.K. relative pricing. Well, that's changed with this deal. For $99, the WH-CH730N are a hell of a lot of headphones for the money.

We're big fans of the fit, finish, sound and noise cancelling of the JBL Live 780NC, and this Black Friday deal makes them a great bet if you've got a little more to spend (but still want to maximise those savings).

It has been revealed that the venerable Beats Studio Pro hit different when they're $200 off MSRP. Solid ANC? Check. A cool, stylish look? Check. Good sound quality? That's a royal flush, baby.

Sources indicate that bose might have replaced the QuietComfort headphones with an also reduced pair, but at this price, these are Bose headphones to go for. Excellent ANC for the price, a comfortable fit, and increasingly-rare-these-days physical controls.

It has been revealed that the Nothing Headphone (1) can help you live out your sci-fi dreams while offering solid customizable sound and a great control scheme. Not bad for a Black Friday deal.

According to recent reports, the Momentum 4 have a reputation of being a little... boring. If, that is, you consider some of the best-sounding headphones for the price and 60 hours of battery life boring. I don't — and neither does this massive $120 saving on the Sennheiser Momentum 4.

Sony recently relaunched the original XM4, hence the XM4C. The new cans have upgraded to the latest Bluetooth 6.0, a new removable (and therefore replaceable) battery, and some AI audio upscaling. Look, none of that was strictly necessary, as the XM4 were still fantastic anyway — even in 2026. But new features is never a bad thing.

Industry observers note that remember I remarked up top that Bose made newly introduced headphones to replace its more affordable model? They're right here, and $160 off! If you want some snazzier colors and a new design, you've found the cans for you — the Bose QuietComfort Headphones 2nd gen.

Sonos's first attempt at headphones was a solid one, earning a coveted 4.5 stars in our Sonos Ace review. We loved the sound and noise cancelling, the battery life, the design and the integration with other Sonos gear. If you're an existing Sonos user, this is the deal for you.

The Beats 360 are the latest in the Beats range and the headphones to buy if you need something to soundtrack your workouts. Not only are they water- and sweatproof, but they feature replaceable ear and head pads. That means you can choose the most comfortable pads for your workout, and swap out if they get gross from, well, your sweaty self.

Sony's XM6 weigh very little and sound excellent — and now you can get them for $100 off. As you'll see in our Sony WH-1000XM6 review, they offer excellent noise cancellation, improved call quality over prior models, and an epic 30 hours of battery life.

Industry observers note that pure. Class. That's how I'd describe the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3. And I'd know, because I own and use a set of them on a near daily basis at home. The Px7 S3 have a warmer, bassier tune than the reference-tuned Px8 S2 (also on sale), but you still get that Bowers refinement and fidelity. Oh, and they're built like you'd expect from a luxury audio brand: bloomin' marvellously.

According to recent reports, this isn't the lowest we've seen the AirPods Max 2 drop ($399)... but it's damn well close. And given these are the latest, greatest, and still rather new'n'shiny flagships from Apple no less, $130 is a surprisingly good chunk of cash off.

Industry observers note that look, I'm a Bowers fanboy, I'll admit it. And I own the Px8 S2. So I have no problem giving some sage advice here: buy the Px8 S2, you won't regret it. Yes, they're pricey, but they make up for it with beautiful, spacious, high fidelity sound, exquisite build quality and strong ANC.

In a recent development, scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Sources indicate that plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Sources indicate that even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Industry observers note that most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA states the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

In a recent development, if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Sources indicate that spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

In a recent development, if you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

Buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

New Yorkers woke up this Thanksgiving morning to drizzly, gray skies along with winds that had sidewalks covered in dead, yellow leaves, though the weather throughout the pre-noon hours was hardly the fearsome nor’easter blast that prompted the postponement till Saturday of Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Still, with wind levels of up to 23 mph – and gusts considerably stronger – the postponement appears to have been justified, and the worst of the storm is yet to come.

The impact of the postponement on performances that had been scheduled for today – marching bands, celebrity appearances, the massive Broadway medley involving nine different shows – was still be dealt with as of this morning. Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer of the parade, told the Today show this morning that organizers are “actively working through all the pieces of our parade, but I have to say there’s an overwhelming positive response.” Related Stories News Mayor Zohran Mamdani Claims Famed Balloons Will Soar Again At Rescheduled Macy's Parade: "It's The Only Inflation We Support In Fresh York City" News Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed To Saturday Due To Severe Weather; NBC Will Rerun 2025 Parade On Thursday.

Coss continued, “Our performers, our talent, our performance groups, our bands, we’re all coming together to try to figure this out, and we’re optimistic that we’re going to have a really successful parade on Saturday morning.” Watch on Deadline.

Sources indicate that while Coss didn’t specify which performances are on schedule, Deadline can confirm that the Broadway medley that was planned in lieu of the traditional individual show performances is a go for Saturday. What Macy’s is calling the “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” will go on as planned, with performers from The Lost Boys, The Rocky Horror Show, Wicked, Schmigadoon!, Aladdin, The Book of Mormon and Chicago confirmed. (Hamiilton and the 30th-anniversary tribute to Rent have not weighed in yet, but sources say they are expected to participate).

Paddington the Musical is confirmed to participate in the Saturday broadcast as a separate float, as originally intended.

On Instagram today, Sherri Shepherd, currently portraying Genie in Broadway’s Aladdin, wrote, “Winds won’t stop our participation in the Macys 100 Thanksgiving Day Parade, so tune in Saturday at 8:30am on NBC to catch myself and the cast of Aladdin perform!!”.

In a recent development, on the Schmigadoon! IG page, Brad Oscar, dressed and in character as the Mayor, said in a video, “As mayor of Schmigadoon, I have a proclamation: The Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed until Saturday at 8:30 a.m. on NBC. See you there.”.

The Book of Mormon had a simple message on its IG page about the date switch: “Ready and psyched.”.

As for other non-Broadway performers originally scheduled for Thursday, reports are filtering in piecemeal on whether they’ll make the move to Saturday. The Latest York Post has reported that Smash Mouth will perform, and Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete are expected as well, as are the Radio City Rockettes. Other announcements should be coming in over the next day or two.

Sources indicate that as for the marching bands, again, piecemeal reports. Texas’ Pride of Pearland Marching Band reportedly raised an extra $350,000 in community donations to cover the additional housing and transportation costs to stay until Saturday, while other marching bands were either still scrambling or had made the decision to bow out of the event due to logistics. In the latter group are the Campo Verde High School Marching Band and some members of the Bowling Green State University Marching Band that were participating in a all-star band group.

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two major improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Industry observers note that precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

Industry observers note that this expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

In a recent development, when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company states this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

In a recent development, I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the newly introduced speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that owners are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Industry observers note that have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

Recent findings suggest that if you want the most portable way to listen to music on the go, then the best earbuds are a fantastic way to do it. They're tiny, often comfortable, and offer noise cancellation to keep the sounds of the outside world at bay.

Industry observers note that at the moment, the AirPods Pro 3 take the crown. But we've spent hundreds of hours testing earbuds to find out which are the best around if you want more than just Apple's offering. They come at a range of different price points to suit any budget, too.

Each entry on the list has a quick read section, giving you a brief overview of the buds, followed by longer reviews so that you can get a better idea of how they perform. So let's get straight into it. These are the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

We've spent 20 years testing the best earbuds (and the worst; you don't know until they're in your ears) to help you find your next set of portable audio companions.

The expertise comes from a few places, including our expert reviewers Erin Bashford and Nikita Achanta, who lead our audio testing. Then there's me, Tammy Rodgers, and I've been testing audio equipment for over half a decade, including a time as Tom's Guide's Audio Editor.

Before any earbuds make their way to this guide, here's how we put them through their paces to make sure we only recommend sets we truly believe in and would use ourselves.

According to recent reports, when you're looking for new earbuds, there's a whole range of terminology brands will use to talk about specs and performance. To make things a bit easier, these are the most common terms that come up, and what they mean for you.

It has been revealed that most earbuds come with Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). It uses audio magic and some very clever algorithms to quiet the outside world and make your commute more manageable.

According to recent reports, the earbuds have mics on the outside to pick up external noise. As this passes into your ear, the earbuds generate an opposing frequency to cancel the sound before you hear it. Sometimes this can change the sound of your music, so we'll report when the ANC is either too weak or too invasive.

Recent findings suggest that the EQ, or equalization, allows you to customize the way the earbuds sound. Usually, this means a series of sliders or dials in the companion smartphone app for adjusting the bass, mids or treble. Some manufacturers give you preset EQ options, which save you from getting lost in sliders or graphs.

It has been revealed that these are the different sounds that make up your music. You'll generally see them divided into three simple sections: the lows, the mids, and the highs. The lows are the bass frequencies. Think bass guitars and kick drums. You want them to be impactful and low.

It has been revealed that the mids are the main parts of your music, like vocals, guitars, and synths. Because they're so notable, you want them to be thick and wide. Finally, the highs are cymbals and other higher sounds. These should be crisp and clear.

Tammy is one of Tom's Guide's Buying Guide Editors. She also spends a great deal of her time testing the best earbuds, evaluating them for sound, ANC, comfort and battery life. She's always got at least three pairs of earbuds to choose from at her desk.

According to recent reports, erin is a proud music nerd and needs the best earbuds around. Whether it's eardrum-shedding nu-metal or tranquil folk, she'll listen to it. If a pair of earbuds has awesome sound quality, bouncy ANC and are comfortable? It's an immediate recommendation, regardless of price or brand.

As a music nerd, Nikita is always listening to music. As a reviews writer, she tests earbuds by pushing battery life to the limit and analyzing performance across various genres to answer the question: Are they good value for money? She listens to music almost throughout the day and plays guitar and bass, so she knows how to determine whether a pair of buds reproduces sound well.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

In a recent development, the AirPods Pro 3 are the latest version of Apple's popular flagship earbuds. The stem-like design remains, but you get better battery life, an improved fit and more detailed sound. This makes them a worthy upgrade from the AirPods Pro 2, and the gold standard for wireless earbuds. Plus, the Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate monitor and Live Translation (if you have a compatible iPhone).

In a recent development, the AirPods Pro 2 were excellent, but soon aged out compared to the competition. Now, the AirPods Pro 3 have arrived to conquer all and lay waste to Sony and Bose. And, despite a couple of minor flaws, they're currently the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

These are the very best earbuds that Apple has ever made. They've got some key updates over the previous model, for one. There's the extended battery life of eight hours, improved sound quality, and superior noise canceling to keep the noise of your commute at bay.

It has been revealed that those upgrades have materialized in a pair of buds that stun in sound and make sure that your office is a whole lot more tolerable when you're getting on with your day. They lose out to the Sony and Bose due to a lack of codec support for Android devices, but there really is nothing better if you're an iPhone user.

In a recent development, the AirPods Pro 3 improve on the old model in the sound department. They've still got Apple's more neutral sound signature built in, but find more detail and extra bass depth than the older pair.

They've got a very solid soundstage as well. They're on par with the Sony buds, and better than the Bose alternatives — although there are still options out there that sound better.

Spatial Audio for movies with an Apple TV is still a great way to watch your content, and just as easy to connect up. It works well for music as well, especially when you listen to your music on Apple Music.

According to recent reports, the buds have been shrunk this time around, and as a result, have a very comfortable fit. The silicone eartips have been infused with foam for a softer and more comfortable finish, and they mold better to the inner part of your ear.

Industry observers note that that means you can wear them for extended periods of time. The sweat and water resistance means you won't have to worry about wearing them when you go to work out, either, hitting an IP57 rating this time around.

The AirPods Pro have always had 'good enough' ANC; powerful but not exceptional. But that changed with the Pro 3, which now almost compete with the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, but don't quite beat out Bose's buds.

Still, it's very good and blocks out all the major noises of your commute or your busy office. It's on par with the Sony WF-1000XM6 — both are excellent noise-canceling options.

Transparency mode is very good as well, and boosts the battery life by another couple of hours. Nice.

There isn't an app for the AirPods Pro 3, but you can easily adjust their settings from the iPhone settings menu. There, you'll find all their features along with options to update the firmware and change the sound.

Although you can pair the AirPods Pro 3 to an Android phone, I wouldn't really recommend it. You get the bare minimum on a non-Apple phone; a wireless connection. You can't adjust settings, so I'd only suggest the AirPods with an Android phone if you're in a bind.

Much like on the Apple Watch, the battery life for the AirPods has remained stuck for years, allowing the competition to lead ahead. The AirPods 3 Pro buck the trend and, for once, increase the per-bud battery life up to eight hours of ANC listening.

That's a two-hour increase and puts them almost in line with the Sony and Bose sets. If you switch over to the transparency mode, you get 10 hours of battery life, more than pretty much anything else at their price point. That also means you can use the new Live Translation feature for longer.

Recent findings suggest that the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds boast excellent sound quality, customizable EQ, and great battery life. Noise cancellation excels, and the design is also great. These are a highly recommended upgrade for superior quiet and sound control.

It has been revealed that when following up on a highly successful pair of earbuds, there are a couple of things you do. First, you make things better — more features, better sound quality. Then you improve the design — make the fit better, improve the looks.

In a recent development, that’s the WF-1000XM6, Sony’s follow-up to the WF-1000XM5. The AirPods of this generation make a better case for your money if you wield an iPhone, but the XM6 are great for just about everyone else. Just like their predecessor, they’re a fantastic all-rounder, with great specs, sound and ANC.

Our four-star review highlights that they’re not entirely perfect. The latest case design is a bit odd and makes fitting them into a pocket a chore, and they’re more expensive than the previous model, but those are our only major criticisms.

It has been revealed that the sound quality is, as you might expect for something from the WF-1000X series, very good, with support for LDAC. Sony’s excellent DSEE Extreme audio upscaler is here as well, and works a treat. The ANC boasts a massive improvement, too, although Bose still has Sony beat for out-and-out noise performance.

They’re a wonderful pair of comfortable buds with plenty of battery life — there’s little more you could ask for, apart from a discount.

It has been revealed that they may seem on the expensive side, but the upgrades in sound performance make them totally worth it. Sony is known for a warmer sound profile on their headphones, and these are a total joy to listen to.

They are only made better by using the personalized EQ settings on the earbuds, and there’s seriously no genre that these buds can’t cope with.

Your favorite songs will sound a lot more detailed, and it’s really awesome to get a studio sound from earbuds instead of having to rely on studio headphones to do the job.

These earbuds are superbly comfortable, and you get a bunch of different eartip options in the box to get the best seal and best security. You can do a fit test to make sure everything fits.

I can wear these buds for hours at a time — they’re seriously comfortable, and they’re lightweight so they never weigh me down.

Industry observers note that ANC differs depending on personal experience with these buds. My own experience was amazing, and I couldn’t fault them at all. They made a long travel day on a plane, train, and bus completely silent.

However, another one of my colleagues who tried them out was still able to hear the sounds of traffic moving around. I think it’s all about the eartip fit, so this is an extremely key process to complete.

If you buy this set, just make sure you use the Optimal Earbud Tips feature in the Sound Connect App to get the best fit, and ensure your ANC is working properly.

According to recent reports, the Sound Connect app is one of the most user-friendly I’ve tried. Once you get the hang of things and organize the app to suit the settings you need to use the most, it’s incredibly handy and makes using the earbuds so much better.

The app is where you do all the earbud fit tests and personalized EQ tests to make the overall experience with the buds so much better.

Recent findings suggest that you get eight hours of battery per bud with ANC and 24 hours with the charging case. This is pretty standard and matches up with Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 and the Sony WF-1000XM5.

The A100 SE are all about sound — pure and simple. There's no feature bloat, no extra AI things, just a pair of great-sounding earbuds with epic battery life. The ANC has fallen behind the competition a little this time around, but they're a great pick for a fantastic price.

Industry observers note that the first Cambridge A100 are some of my favorite wireless earbuds — and the SE version are no different. They’re refined and classy in their sound, as befits a legacy British Hi-Fi brand. The soundstage is expansive and well layered, and vocals shine. Erin loved the dynamism and vibrancy in her review, noting the accuracy and faithfulness of their representation. High praise indeed.

It has been revealed that we had no problems with the comfort as well, and wore them extensively during the testing period. The case is compact and well-shaped (perfect for fitting them into a tighter pocket), and the app is useful and well laid out, though simplistic.

Industry observers note that there are just a couple of problems. The ANC isn’t quite up there with other options at a similar price, and the Dolby Atmos mode is, like, bad. But beyond those two bugbears, the A100 SE are the perfect successor to some of our favorite earbuds and a top-notch value pick.

According to recent reports, cambridge has fired a warning shot at just about every other audio manufacturer with the A100 SE. The first model sounded good, but these sound even better. We love how dynamic and clear the buds sound, and the seven-band custom EQ means you can really dial them in.

They sound better even than more expensive earbuds, and take the fight to options that cost $100-$150 more. That’s the focus of the buds: excellent sound, forget the frills.

Recent findings suggest that there’s warmth here, but it doesn’t overshadow the rest of the sound. Everything is still very clear and expansive, with solid instrument separation. We’re big fans of the sound.

We scored the buds well for comfort, thanks to their smooth shape and range of different eartips. For the most part, we were able to wear them for long periods without them getting uncomfortable. We didn’t want to rip them out after the workday.

But those with small ears might struggle a little more. These aren’t small buds, and for one tester, they pressed on some parts of their ear. They weren’t uncomfortable, but they knew they were there.

The ANC isn’t going to win them any awards. It’s fine and blocks out some noise, but it’s not as all-encompassing as other options available. If you’re looking for something that blocks out everything, then you might want to think about Sony’s similarly priced options.

Still, if ANC isn’t a priority but you still want some noise blocking, then you won’t find anything to complain about — and the noise-canceling compromise is worth making for that excellent sound.

Sources indicate that cambridge’s app is fine, but we did have some problems with some of the features. It became a little buggy at times, with some features not working as they should. A quick restart fixed the matter, but it’s still worth mentioning.

What we really liked, however, was the complete omission of extra feature bloat. There’s everything you might need — an EQ, ANC controls, and that surround mode — but there’s nothing extra. No AI feature, no voice control thing, just what you actually need when using the buds. That’s refreshing.

Industry observers note that battery life is a particular strength of Cambridge's headphones and earbuds. Here, we’ve got 39 hours on tap, 10 hours of bud life. Sources indicate that everything charges up swiftly, and we found that the battery figures matched up to expectations when we did all of our testing. If you want something that lasts a long time, the A100 SE are a great option.

It has been revealed that the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the fitness lover's dream. A very comfortable, secure fit so that they stay in place no matter how you move around, and great sound quality to power your workouts. The built-in heart rate monitor is a great cherry on top.

Thanks to their excellent earhook, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 aren't going anywhere when you do your exercise. It can be a challenge to get them in place, but they're very stable once in.

In a recent development, the transparency modes work well enough, although I found that voices occasionally became fuzzy or tricky to hear depending on the surrounding noise. A shame, but not a deal breaker.

The battery life of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 is exemplary. They feature 10 hours of battery life in the buds themselves, beating out many other options on this list.

Sources indicate that that's perfect for long-distance runners and cyclists, or gym-goers who want something that will take them to the gym, last through their exercise, and then take them home again. We found those battery life claims were true in our review. Pop them in the charging case for 45 hours of staying power.

Improving on almost every metric compared to the original model (except battery), the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 are an in-ear noise-canceling triumph. Boosts to ANC and sound quality make them an even better buy than the first model, and the price hasn't increased to match the improved performance.

The Noble Fokus Amadeus are all about one thing and one thing only — their sound quality. Sound quality that blows just about everything else you can buy out of the water. Their ANC is very good, and they're very comfortable, but you buy these for their sound quality.

And you will want a pair, because they've dethroned other excellent-sounding earbuds with their incredibly well-rounded sound signature that dishes out masterful amounts of detail while providing plenty of low-end punch.

For the price, this is about as close to wired earbuds as you're going to get. The crisp detail is utterly sublime, their mids are fat and juicy, and the bass is tight, controlled, and impactful. Recent findings suggest that the price means they're out of reach for many users, but as I discovered in my testing, they're well worth their higher price thanks to a very good all-round package. The battery is good, and the ANC matches up — there's very little to get sad about here.

Recent findings suggest that the absolute best thing about the Noble Fokus Amadeus is their sound profile. Thanks to the Audiodo profile in the app it means they sound amazing for everyone too, catering the sound for specific hearing needs.

Recent findings suggest that there are details in my tracks I'd not heard for a while thanks to the impressive detail, and the mids bring plenty of body to listening. The bass kicks and barks with impressive control, notably adding more for drum and bass in particular.

The sound is effortlessly spaced apart for a wide soundstage, and the instruments are very well separated. They sound better than absolutely everything on this list — they're hard to get hold of, but it's worth every single effort when you do.

CMF's latest pair of budget buds are sub-$50 heroes. They pack in loads of premium features, like great customization and even a form of spatial audio. They sound great, fit well, and come in a range of different colors. What's not to like?

Sources indicate that the sound is the most impressive thing here, though. They sound like a pair of buds that cost loads more, and once you’ve gone through the Dirac sound tuning, there’s very little better for under $100. Premium buds — low price.

Thanks to CMF’s use of Dirac, the CMF Buds 2 sound excellent. While the core sound is very good, with plenty of bass for impact and revealing detail for interest, the EQ settings kick things up a notch. We’ve described it as “breathing newly introduced life into your songs” — and you’d be hard-pressed to find something at this price that sounds better.

It has been revealed that they’re great for a wide range of genres as a result. We spun up everything from the heaviest of metal to breezy folk and classical, and the buds didn’t skip a beat. They’re as meaty as they are delicate — extremely impressive considering the price.

Recent findings suggest that there’s nothing else that sounds like this at the low price point at which they sit. Even without Dirac, they’re impressive — although you’ll want to run the tuning engine to get the most out of them possible.

Sources indicate that thanks to a multitude of fitting options in the box and a great bud design, the CMF Buds 2 are very comfortable. There are three different sizes, and we found that the ‘small’ size option was perfect for even very small ears.

There are comfier buds out there, but we had little problem wearing them all day during our testing. More expensive buds might feel slightly nicer in the ear, but these still feel great for the price.

Industry observers note that you can’t expect Bose-level ANC for $50, but you’ll be immediately impressed by the noise-canceling packed into the CMF Buds 2. It does a very good job of keeping the outside world at bay, with some very impressive noise blocking.

It has been revealed that the transparency mode is good too, making it easy to hear what's going on without a robotic edge. They cut down slightly with the ANC during calls — while your voice will be clear, your call partner will be able to hear everything going on around you.

It has been revealed that the Nothing X app is excellent. It's super simple to navigate, with easy access to all the features in the buds. There’s a home screen, and then various menus that are clearly labelled. It’s a must-install if you pick up the CMF Buds 2.

This is where you find the Dirac tuning menu, as well as other settings. Those include the ANC settings, fit test, spatial audio, and touch control settings.

11 hours of use in the buds is very solid indeed, and our testing showed no reason to dispute CMF's claims. The case contains 55 hours of use, so you can charge the buds about four times from empty. This is good battery life for buds, better than even some of the more premium options.

Samsung's latest buds bring a less AirPods-like case design and excellent sound quality to the table. Some settings and options are locked off for everyone but Galaxy device owners, but they're a great option for the Samsung faithful.

Not one to miss out on a good earbud battle, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro bring a whole host of features to the Samsung crowd who want something that seamlessly integrates with their phone.

Sources indicate that they sound great, and Samsung’s audio upscaling tech is almost as good as Sony’s for improving weaker streams from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music. That looks like the place Samsung has put the most work into the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, improving massively over the older model.

Industry observers note that not quite as much work seems to have gone into the battery life, unfortunately. There are only around seven hours on tap with ANC turned on, which lags behind the key competition like the eight hours of the AirPods Pro 3. Still, you get more charge in the case at 30 hours.

It has been revealed that samsung has also packed in some very solid ANC, with loads of clever modes if you wield a Galaxy handset. That’s where their true value lies. There are a bunch of features that only Samsung users will appreciate, like AI translation that only works with Galaxy phones.

If you’re a Galaxy phone user, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro were likely already on your shortlist. Thanks to our testing, we can tell you that they’re a great pair of buds that’ll pair with your device perfectly.

“Overall, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound utterly divine” is how Erin finished off the sound portion of the buds review. That’s thanks to rich bass, excellent mids, and great vocals, giving you a top-notch audio experience.

Detail heads might prefer the slightly tighter AirPods or Sony WF-1000XM6, but these sound better than the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. Their AI sound enhancement works great with lower-quality streams as well.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to some solid shaping, the Buds 4 Pro are comfortable to wear for long periods of time. There are plenty of fitting options in the box as well to make sure that you’ll find the best fit for you, no matter what shape your ear canals are.

Some with smaller ears might find their slightly larger bodies tighter, but it’s not enough to make them in any way uncomfortable.

The noise canceling is excellent, blocking out all the noise that we could throw at them. They perform about the same as the AirPods and Sony competition, making for more relaxing journeys while wearing them.

Transparency mode is also good, and doesn’t make any of the incoming noise sound robotic. The ANC performance might not be quite as impressive as the Bose buds, but it’s more than a match for the Sony and Apple alternatives.

Some of the headline features, like the AI settings and call enhancement, are only available for Galaxy S23 models and newer. The buds use the Samsung settings menu itself rather than a dedicated app on these devices, and it works well.

Sources indicate that there is a Samsung app for other devices, and it's fine. You can control the ANC and other settings, and upgrade the firmware. Still, there are better app experiences for non-Galaxy owners, like the Sony and Bose apps.

Not every pair of earbuds we test can land on the best list — otherwise, this would just be a list of earbuds that are available to buy. But some are still pretty good and worth considering if you need more options.

Before we make a recommendation about any pair of wireless earbuds, we want to make sure that we've put them through their paces. It helps us find out how good they'll be when you find them in your hands, and makes sure that we can pen our informative, buying advice-packed reviews.

It's all work — no fun. Listening to our favorite music for hours on end to test the sound, taking the earbuds out and about on day trips to test their long-term comfort and ANC algorithm. In all seriousness, we put a lot of effort into making sure that you'll be happy with a purchase you make after reading our buying guides and reviews.

Here are the key factors in our testing and how we evaluate each pair of earbuds that falls across our desks.

Industry observers note that earbuds are going to be jammed directly into your ear holes, so one of the most vital things that we test is how comfortable they are over long periods of time, and how difficult it is to dial in the fit. How many bud bits do you get in the box, and are they easy to fit on the buds? Are they loose? Are there extra fitting options like earhooks?

Industry observers note that to find out, we put the buds through their paces. We try out a range of the tips that come with the budsto find the perfect fit that makes the ANC excellent and sound good. After all, if they don't seal well inside of your ear, you're not going to get the best out of your buds. We report our findings, like how easy it was to get the perfect fit, and how comfy they are when dialed in.

Then we test their long-term comfort. That means wearing them for hours during a work day, so that we can see how they feel when they're worn for hours on end. If they start impacting certain pressure points in the ear, we'll notice, and it'll go into our review. We're looking for earbuds that can't be felt during wear, so that you forget you're wearing them.

According to recent reports, this is my favorite thing to test. Hours and hours of my favorite tunes played into my ears while I work, and I don't have to make excuses to my boss about why I need to be doing it. Excellent news. When we test the audio quality of a pair of buds, we play the Tom's Guide testing playlist on Qobuz so that we can get a good picture of how they sound with some top-quality hi-res tracks to put them through their paces.

Recent findings suggest that we listen at first in a quieter environment so that we can get an idea of how they sound in a vacuum without the ANC to cause potential problems. We compare the earbuds to the sound profiles of those in the best list above, and then we write down our findings for the full review.

In a recent development, then, we take the earbuds out with the ANC to see if it changes the sound. It might all sound like we're having fun, but there is a point to it all. It gives us a clear picture of the buds' performance in an everyday use case, so that we can see how they'll serve you if you decide you'd like to buy a pair.

Pretty much every pair of earbuds that you can buy today comes with some form of ANC (unless you buy some of the very cheapest ones at the very end of a lengthy Amazon search, you madman), and we want to make sure that it performs well in a variety of use cases.

How do we do it? By taking the earbuds with us wherever we go. That could mean on all our daily commutes, to see if they perform well on the train, or out for hikes so we can see how well they handle normal atmospheric noise. Maybe we're going on a flight — then we can test how well they handle loud engines and crying children.

Once we've thoroughly tested how much noise they block, we also test the transparency modes when we go to buy our tickets or a bag of candies from the grocery store. We look out for how clear the voice of our conversation partner is, and whether they're audible through any other noise. We're also looking out for the quality of the audio that's being pumped in. Is it too loud? Again, we note down our findings for the review.

In a recent development, finally, we want to make sure that the ANC doesn't change the sound of the music too much. After all, you want your music to sound great, and if the ANC changes things too much, it can create annoying sonic challenges.

It has been revealed that given that your earbuds are often going to pull double duty as a form of hands-free calling system, we want to ensure that they're going to be good at it. We make a whole bunch of calls to check things out.

We're looking out for a couple of different things. First of all, we want to make sure that we can hear our call partner well, and that they're coming through clearly. We listen out for clarity and judge whether we can hear them properly throughout the duration of the call, and whether their voice sounds natural.

Recent findings suggest that then we ask our call partners how we sound. Can they hear us properly, or do the noises of our environment make it hard to hear what we're saying? We note down our findings, and then we report back on them in our review to give you an idea of how they'll perform if you want to take (or make) a call.

We know that manufacturers sometimes have a habit of overestimating their battery life figures. To make sure that you're getting the best information possible, we spend the time testing the battery life claims and whether they ring true. We listen to the buds for hours on end, and count how many hours we used them before they needed to go back into their case. We do this with ANC turned on and with the volume at a comfortable level.

Sources indicate that for charging cases and very long-lasting buds, we extrapolate battery data in a different way. We measure how long we've used them, and then compare that with how much life we've got left. This gives us a good picture of how the battery is going to last in the long run, and whether you'll get those rated claims.

According to recent reports, hopefully, we've managed to curate a list of wireless earbuds that hit the mark for you. But if you're still not sure how to choose between them, these are some additional pointers.

What do you want out of your buds?

In a recent development, there are as many reasons to buy earbuds as there are earbuds themselves. You need to work out what you're looking for first and foremost — it's why I've divided the list up into the most crucial headline features.

Recent findings suggest that do you want the best sound, and would you be willing to give up some battery life and pay a bit more for it? If not, then you should go for the best earbuds overall, but if you don't mind some compromise, then you should go for the best-sounding earbuds.

It's crucial to make a list of the features that are most important to you, and then work out from there which of the earbuds on the list fit those criteria the best. After all, what might be the best for one person might not be the best for you.

Do you want headphones or earbuds?

According to recent reports, if you're looking for the most compact, easily transported audio device around, then the best earbuds are probably going to be right for you. But there are a couple of things to remember: they're going to live inside your ears, and not everyone likes the feeling of in-ears after longer periods of listening.

If you'd prefer something more comfortable for longer periods of wear that offers more battery life, and potentially better audio quality, you should consider some of the best wireless headphones. They might cost a bit more, but you might be more comfortable.

In a recent development, repairability is becoming ever more vital, as we try to find new ways to lengthen the life of our devices, but also look after the planet that we call home. Repairing products is great for both, and it's important to consider it when buying new tech.

In a recent development, unfortunately, earbuds are one of those products that are extremely rarely user-repairable. Thanks to their size and the amount of tech that companies have to pack into their buds, it's generally impossible to make the insides accessible to you or me.

Sources indicate that not all is lost, however — some manufacturers do offer some form of repair service, so you don't have to worry if your buds stop working. But this is still pretty rare, so if this is a priority for you, it's worth picking up a pair of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2.

According to recent reports, there are seven user-repairable components; they cost less than $100 and come in two colors. Tom's Guide Managing Editor James Frew rated the first generation, but they weren't available in the U.S. That all changed with the Fairbuds 2, which you can buy directly from Fairphone.

Industry observers note that I talk about this on our best headphones list, but I think it's worth reiterating here. It's easy to get hooked on frequency response graphs and numbers, and think you're getting a surefire cheat code to finding the best-sounding earbuds.

You'll spot them as a pair of numbers in spec lists, like "15 Hz-22 kHz." The first number is how low the earbuds can go, and the second is how high they can go.

According to recent reports, you might think that finding a pair with the greatest frequency range is going to net you a pair of excellent-sounding earbuds. While that can be true, it's not worth seeking out. Just because a pair of earbuds can go really low doesn't mean they're good at replicating those frequencies, and neither does it tell you about what's going on in the music itself.

There's only one way to really tell how good a pair of earbuds is — and that's to give them a listen. Or, of course, you could read one of our excellent and informative earbuds reviews.
