The Firefox browser app shown on a smartphone in front of the Firefox logo.

Recent findings suggest that mozilla’s Firefox team now spends 27% of its effort fixing security flaws, up from about 10% a year ago, Firefox head Ajit Varma told Business Insider. OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla free access to models that are finding more complex bugs.

Industry observers note that mozilla’s Firefox team now spends 27% of its effort fixing security flaws, up from about 10% a year ago, Firefox head Ajit Varma told Business Insider. The rise comes as AI models find more bugs in the browser.

Varma remarked OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla, a nonprofit, “a lot of tokens for free”. Their models, he said, “are finding more and more complicated vulnerabilities within our browser.”.

It has been revealed that in April, Mozilla patched 271 Firefox bugs found by Anthropic’s Mythos. OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Cyber model has since turned up 81 more. Rival browsers face the same surge: Chrome patched a record 429 bugs in June.

Varma still thinks the pace of AI gives his team “enough time” to fix problems before the next leap. He is also using AI to make Firefox faster and stop memory leaks.

“There’s a lot of routine activities that we don’t necessarily need humans to do and that AI does really well because it’s relentless; it doesn’t get tired,” he noted.

According to recent reports, others are less relaxed. Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella warned last week that AI-found bugs mean more outages, as companies rush out fixes faster than they can test them.

Microsoft indicates China’s Salt Typhoon and North Korean hackers now use ARTEX

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, Upcoming York.
  • Industry observers note that state-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft says.
  • The list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, Upcoming York.

Industry observers note that state-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft says. Microsoft Threat Intelligence named the groups in a report published on Wednesday.

The list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean. Two more clusters, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358, are also on it. Microsoft states state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers use ARTEX to speed up network scans, credential attacks, and attacks on web apps.

“Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes,” Microsoft wrote.

The report landed hours after US media tied ARTEX to the hack of three US spy agencies, as Jonathan Greig reported for The Record.

Sources indicate that US agencies believe Salt Typhoon breached at least nine telecoms groups in 2024, The Record noted. That hack allegedly reached phones used by Donald Trump and JD Vance. A US House report later said Chinese carriers were still inside American phone networks.

According to recent reports, crystal Typhoon is newer. It was first seen in late 2023 and goes after government networks and critical infrastructure through edge devices and firewalls, TechRadar reported.

Sources indicate that microsoft had already linked Storm-0940 to the ConnectWise supply chain attack. The latest report adds numbers from its campaigns. In one, Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 a minute. In several intrusions, the attackers had privileged access less than three hours after they first went after a target.

In another case, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Sources indicate that A GitHub user called Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese interface in July. The developer took it down in October, but other developers kept publishing their own versions. This month, the Chinese security firm ThreatBook claimed ownership and started selling access to “ARTEX Pro”.

The attacker sets the targets. One AI model breaks the job into goals. A planner agent then hands short tasks to worker agents with a real shell and hacking tools. A reporter agent writes up what worked. ARTEX can run on almost any large language model, including ones stripped of their guardrails. That means no single AI provider’s safety controls can stop it, Microsoft states.

The FBI warned about ARTEX earlier this month.

“ARTEX does not introduce upcoming attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

In a recent development, attackers can change the tool’s IP addresses and user agent strings, so blocking those alone will not work. The steadiest sign is behaviour: many varied requests in a short burst, and quick moves to the next step. ARTEX does nothing to hide that activity by default.

Microsoft also suggests honeypots, tarpits, and fake wins. A fake win demonstrates the agent false proof that its job is done, so it stops. It recommends rate limits, phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in, and replacing any secret that leaks into code. The report also points customers to Microsoft’s own products, including Defender XDR and its Perception security agents.

As seen above, Health introduces brand latest Insights, Longevity, and Browse tabs that replace the previous options and include a variety of fresh UI elements like a top navigation row, personalized prompts and coaching, educational videos, and a lot more.

Calendar also now shows the year at the top of the screen next to the current month, and has updated the ‘Today’ button to show the current date instead.

Safari introduces an optional new design for tabs: Vertical Tabs. You can enable these inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Safari for a different approach to tabs across iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Here’s an example of vertical tabs on iPhone Duo.

Vertical Tabs won’t be for everyone, but they’ve proven popular in other browsers, so it’s great to see Safari add the option.

Song artwork is now able to break the constraints of a square and blend seamlessly into the scrolling lyrics view. Here are examples from Beta Profiles on X:.

Latest Update: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

It has been revealed that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash upcoming competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is vital because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Sources indicate that recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The firm’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s notable to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

According to recent reports, we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

Sources indicate that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

According to recent reports, last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

It has been revealed that to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a upcoming instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Sources indicate that though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

In a recent development, these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Industry observers note that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In a recent development, in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted prepares for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

It has been revealed that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Industry observers note that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

According to recent reports, what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

Rockstar staff vote 75% against union recognition a week after GTA VI

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork featuring Jason and Lucia.
  • Rockstar Games staff in the UK have voted against recognising a union, a week after the studio launched Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • About 1,600 staff below director level could vote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork featuring Jason and Lucia.

Rockstar Games staff in the UK have voted against recognising a union, a week after the studio launched Grand Theft Auto VI. Three in four votes went against a recognition deal with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union. The Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) announced the result on Thursday.

About 1,600 staff below director level could vote. Of those, 1,544 took part, a turnout of 93.2%, Chris Kerr reported for Vertical Slice, which broke the result. The ballot ran from 12 to 26 November.

The split was 75.3% against and 24.7% in favour across the Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee, and London offices, GamesIndustry.biz reported. IGN put the count at 1,163 votes against and 381 for.

A yes vote would have made the branch the largest recognised union in the UK games industry. It would have set up formal talks on pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions. Staff would also have had a say on HR policies and on how Rockstar uses generative AI, Vertical Slice reported.

The union already exists, and staff can still join it. The result means management does not have to hold regular meetings with its representatives. Under UK law, the union cannot apply for recognition again for three years, according to GamesIndustry.biz.

“Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues,” the IWGB noted in a statement.

Industry observers note that the union said the result “isn’t a sign to retreat”. It will keep pushing for pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against AI and layoffs.

“This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong,” Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar’s head of publishing, remarked in a statement.

It has been revealed that the vote follows a long dispute. In October 2025, Rockstar fired more than 30 staff, all IWGB members. The studio states they leaked confidential information in a Discord channel. The union says those talks were protected union activity and accuses Rockstar of union busting.

The fired workers took the case to an employment tribunal in Glasgow, which heard closing arguments on 19 November. Their lawyers argued the sackings came soon after an informant remarked union membership was nearing 10% of staff. That is roughly the level needed to apply for recognition. Rockstar’s counsel told the tribunal the workers were “caught red-handed”, Wccftech reported. Judge Lucy Wiseman has not yet ruled.

Sources indicate that the ballot overlapped with the biggest launch in Rockstar’s history. GTA VI made $3.79 billion in a record first day, after it tied Metacritic’s record with a 99. Take-Two has noted the game was built without generative AI.

It has been revealed that black Friday is a great time to save up on your favorite gadgets, but it's also a fantastic time to pick up a new board or card game. I've been playing board games for as long as I can remember — about 20 years now. My first game was Scrabble, which I still play with my family and partner.

Board games have come a long way, and they're still an excellent way to bond with your family and friends. The holidays are almost upon us, so I highly recommend grabbing either a classic or a brand new one this week. As Tom's Guide's resident board games expert, I've rounded up the best Black Friday deals for you.

In a recent development, my favorite deal is on Catan which is 51% off right now. This is a phenomenal and highly addictive strategy game for up to four players. If you want a more simple game to play with kids and adults alike, get the Magnetic Chess Game for just $8.

If you fancy a card game instead, P for Pizza is my top recommendation, and you can get it for $9 today. Or if you're hosting an adults-only games night, you can't go wrong with Cards Against Humanity which is down to $23 for Black Friday.

Industry observers note that regardless of what you're into, there's a deal for everyone, so allow me to take you through the best Black Friday board and card game deals. And let me know in the comments which game you'll be playing!

By day, I review consumer tech for a living. By night, I'm playing either video games or board/card games. I've loved board and card games since I was a child. My favorites are Scrabble, Catan and Monopoly, and I also thoroughly enjoy silly card games like P for Pizza and Herd Mentality.

Recent findings suggest that when I visited my family a couple of months ago, we spent hours playing this Magnetic Chess Game. One player makes a shape with the included string and other players must place their magnetic pieces without touching the others. It's a great game for adults and kids alike.

This is one for whodunnit and murder mystery fans. Clue is discounted for Black Friday, and is a great game to play with friends and family over the holidays. In this murder mystery board game, you and up to six other players act as detectives to solve a murder. You must figure out who committed the crime, the weapon they used, and which room the crime took place in. Other players will try to ruin your strategy by using cards in their hands, and the first person to make an accurate accusation wins.

In a recent development, do you like board games that are equal parts visually aesthetic and fun? Try Azul! It's a tactile game about tile laying. The mosaic tiles are inspired by Portuguese azulejos. It's easy to learn and deceptively deep in strategy, and works great at just about any player count. If you're not feeling the tile laying, there's a chocolate variant and three sequels that offer different rules and shaped pieces.

I'm sure you've played Monopoly hundreds of times (just me? Okay...), but if you haven't, what are you waiting for? Monopoly's an all-time classic. You and up to five other players buy, sell and scheme your way to becoming the richest person alive. You can build houses and hotels and trade these if a player offers you a better deal. Warning: may cause (friendly) arguments!

Few board games come close to being as great as this one. Catan is a highly addictive strategy game for three to four players which turns you into hard-nosed settlers, competing to conquer an island. You must collect resource cards to build roads, village and cities, but collecting them heavily relies on dice rolls and trading with other players. Oh, and there's a resource-stealing robber too to spice things up, so watch out!

When we're having a cozy date night, P for Pizza is a game my partner and I always play. In this fast-paced card game, you have to shout out a word that links the letter on one card to the category on another (on a pile in the middle of the table). For example, a food that starts with G, an actress whose name begins with K, a stringed instrument that starts with S, and so on. You need to be quick to add a slice to your pile, and the first one to form a 'pizza slice' wins.

It has been revealed that need a party game for the holidays? Try Herd Mentality. It's easy to pick up and play as all you need to do is flip a card and read out a random question like, "Who is the most popular female artist of all time?" You and the other players then write down the answer you think will be the most common among the group. If you're in the majority, you win points; if not, you'll be left with the dreaded pink cow of doom. And as someone who adores cows, you don't want to get stuck with this one...

It has been revealed that if you want a fast-paced board/card game where you deduce your fellow players' behavior, The Chameleon is for you. In this game, everyone know a secret word except one hidden imposter. Each player gives a single related clue to prove they belong without revealing too much. The group then votes to unmask the traitor... or Chameleon, if you will. Each round can last as long as the group likes.

According to recent reports, the first time I played You Can't Say UMM was at a board games café with my friends. We laughed so much that our jaws hurt and we had tears running down our faces. In this card game, you have to describe an object to your teammate without saying "Umm" or "Err." The opposing team can catch you out and penalize you. Opponents can also add "rules" to your turn, such as, "Swap seats with a teammate after every correct guess." It's harder than it sounds, and it's a barrel of laughs.

In a recent development, cards Against Humanity is the perfect card game for adults — and to determine who among your friend group has the darkest humor. One player reads a fill-in-the-blank prompt from a black card, and everyone else submits their funniest, most offensive, or absurd white answer card. The reader picks the winner, awarding a point. It can get really horrible really fast — but it's oh so fun.

Industry observers note that my partner and I play Ransom Notes with our friends fairly often. In this game, you and the other players race against a timer to answer outrageous prompts using only a limited handful of random word magnets. Everyone reads their grammatically chaotic sentences aloud while a rotating judge picks the funniest response to award a point. The first to five points (or the number of your choosing) wins!

Signal’s Moxie Marlinspike says AI safety is building mass surveillance

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that moxie Marlinspike, who built Signal, says the way AI companies police misuse is turning into the biggest mass surveillance system ever built.
  • “You’re building a machinery of mass surveillance that is larger and more efficient than any other mass surveillance machinery in history,” Marlinspike mentioned.
  • Industry observers note that he described today’s approach as scoring everything customers do for “badness” and sending the worst to human reviewers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that moxie Marlinspike, who built Signal, says the way AI companies police misuse is turning into the biggest mass surveillance system ever built. He wants the watching pointed at the AI models instead of the people using them, he told Tyler Cowen on Conversations with Tyler. The episode was recorded live at the Progress Conference on 10 October and published on Wednesday.

“You’re building a machinery of mass surveillance that is larger and more efficient than any other mass surveillance machinery in history,” Marlinspike mentioned.

Industry observers note that he described today’s approach as scoring everything customers do for “badness” and sending the worst to human reviewers. TNW reported in September that contractors read real ChatGPT conversations.

Sources indicate that his alternative is to monitor whether the models themselves show bad tendencies. Labs would train narrow models that each spot one kind of behaviour, then use them to check the general models. Cowen asked whether using AI to watch AI really counts, pointing to the Hugging Face breach. Marlinspike said it does.

Recent findings suggest that chatbots invite confession because they feel private, Marlinspike said. In practice, chats end up in a data lake used for training and analysis.

“You feel like you’re having this conversation with this agent or assistant that gets to know you as your friend… but actually, it’s a huge group chat with many, many more people,” he stated.

He runs Confer, a private AI chat service at confer.to. Only the user can read their chats, he noted, and he cannot. Claude and ChatGPT “are not operating private services,” he added, though he said the massive labs could build one.

Asked whether the recent flood of AI maths results could break cryptography, Marlinspike answered: “I don’t know.”.

“If there is some result that just all of public-key cryptography doesn’t work anymore, then the whole internet is in trouble,” he said.

In that worst case, nobody could trust software updates, websites or online banking. He also described milder outcomes, where some algorithms would only need larger keys. Moving to post-quantum encryption took about five years, he said, and a second switch would likely be faster.

On hacking, he expects a painful period before AI gets as good at patching flaws as at finding them. He put the wait at about a year. Cowen doubted that small cities could patch their systems that fast.

Industry observers note that marlinspike remarked Signal knows almost nothing about its users. It cannot see their contacts, group names, profile names, searches, or stickers. WhatsApp uses the Signal protocol to encrypt messages, but much of that other data is not protected, he said. Signal recently moved to block AI agents from reading chats.

Cowen pushed back on privacy more broadly. He stated face scans speed up airports and that CCTV cut murders in São Paulo. Marlinspike said it is hard to argue against a city with a murder problem. He still opposes airport face scanning and argued that law enforcement should stay imperfect.

Cowen also asked what the 2025 Pentagon group chat on Signal had done for the app.

“It made it all worth it for me,” Marlinspike said.

Breaking: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shows running iOS simulators in the Finder sidebar so you can drag files in and out of them.
  • Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down.
  • According to recent reports, or download SimDrop-macos.dmg from GitHub Releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shows running iOS simulators in the Finder sidebar so you can drag files in and out of them.

Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal:.

According to recent reports, or download SimDrop-macos.dmg from GitHub Releases. Requires macOS 15 or later. It is Developer ID signed and notarized. SimDrop isn't on the Mac App Store and can't be: the app and its helper must run unsandboxed to drive simctl and the simulators' folders.

Open SimDrop once. The window is only a settings page showing whether these two one-time approvals are done:.

It has been revealed that after that it works silently in the background, including after a restart. The window can be closed.

After installing or upgrading, open SimDrop once. Replacing the app makes macOS drop its Finder extension (Finder then says the application can't be found) and stop the background helper. launchd refuses to start a helper whose recorded launch constraint came from the old copy (needs LWCR revision, exit 78). Until the new version has been rolled out, no part of SimDrop can run to repair this. A Homebrew postflight_steps can't launch it either, because open fails inside the cask step sandbox. So the cask shows a caveat instead. Opening the app re-registers the extension and makes sure the helper answers with this build's version. If needed, it boots the stale launchd job out and registers the helper again.

Finder moves files when you drag within the same volume and copies only across volumes. File Provider locations live in ~/Library/CloudStorage on your startup disk, so dragging a file from the Desktop into SimDrop moves it. iCloud Drive and Google Drive behave the same way, and File Provider has no API to change this.

According to recent reports, making SimDrop copy by default like a USB drive would require it to be a separate volume (e.g. an FSKit file system), which would be a rewrite.

Paths inside a simulator (~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices//):.

CI (.github/workflows/release.yml) runs when MARKETING_VERSION in project.yml changes on main. It generates the project with XcodeGen, then uses rxliuli/apple-release/dmg to archive, sign with Developer ID, build the DMG, notarize, staple and publish a GitHub Release. The release-macOS environment needs these secrets: APPLE_CERTIFICATE_DEVELOPERID_BASE64, APPLE_CERTIFICATE_DEVELOPERID_PASSWORD, APPLE_API_KEY, APPLE_API_KEY_ID, APPLE_API_ISSUER, and optionally TAP_GITHUB_TOKEN. When it is set, the release also bumps Casks/sim-drop.rb in rxliuli/homebrew-tap.

No provisioning profile is involved. The app group is Team-ID-prefixed (N2X78TUUFG.com.rxliuli.sim-drop, not group.…), which macOS accepts without one.

It has been revealed that app icon: the source is Design/icon-source.png (a full-bleed 1024 squircle with transparent corners). Regenerate the icon set with swift Design/make-icon.swift Design/icon-source.png SimDrop/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset. The script scales the artwork to the 824pt macOS icon grid and adds a drop shadow.

Don't remove the helper's launchd job on a plain uninstall (e.g. uninstall launchctl: in the cask). brew upgrade runs the old version's uninstall step before installing the new one, so the job disappears while the registration still indicates "enabled". The cask only does this on --zap.

Switching between a dev build and an installed release: only one copy should be registered. launchd records a launch constraint (LWCR) for the helper with the signing identity of whichever copy registered it. If that copy differs from the one now on disk (e.g. Apple Development vs Developer ID), launchd refuses to start the helper (last exit reason = OS_REASON_CODESIGNING). Quit the other copy, then run launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.rxliuli.sim-drop.helper and launch the copy you want with --args -reregisterHelper YES. Duplicate extensions (pluginkit -m -v -D -i com.rxliuli.sim-drop.FileProvider) also hide SimDrop from System Settings › Login Items & Extensions.

Logs: log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "com.rxliuli.sim-drop"'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Stefon Walters – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:39AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›.

It has been revealed that I consider myself adventurous, but I often prefer boring when it comes to the stocks I own. I have my fair share of growth stocks, for sure, but my staple "boring" stock is Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%).

Recent findings suggest that although Coca-Cola is up over 40% this year (as of Nov. 24), its main appeal has long been its dividend. It has increased its annual dividend for 64 consecutive years, making it one of the market's premier Dividend Kings ( companies with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend hikes). Considering that and its sustained success, it's a stock I'll never sell.

It has been revealed that you can count on one hand the number of brands more well-known globally than Coca-Cola. Its products (especially its namesake soda) are available in virtually every part of the world, and its asset-light business model enables it to operate efficiently.

Sources indicate that usually, if a company wants distribution somewhere, it needs plants, warehouses, and delivery fleets in that market. In Coca-Cola's case, it relies on bottling and distribution partners to do so. Instead of owning factories and delivery fleets around the world, Coca-Cola sells concentrates and syrups to its partners and lets them do the heavy lifting.

Industry observers note that keeping its business asset-light lets Coca-Cola maintain high margins and an ultra-safe dividend. You don't get to 64 years of dividend increases without consistent, high-margin cash flows.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Industry observers note that not many companies fit the "recession-proof" narrative, but Coca-Cola is one of them. Even when the economy slows and money is tight, people still buy their favorite Coca-Cola brands. That's the beauty of its brand moat.

And despite being the undisputed leader in its space, Coca-Cola hasn't gotten complacent with its drink portfolio. It constantly refines its lineup to adjust to changing consumer preferences. Just six years ago, it had over 400 brands in its portfolio. Today, it has around half of that.

Sources indicate that when you have an option for virtually every occasion, you keep customers in your ecosystem. It's how the tech giant has sustained success for so long.

In a recent development, coca-Cola is a premium business that's priced like one. At the time of this writing, it's trading at 28.9 times its earnings, which is higher than its average over the past few years and higher than the S&P 500's (^GSPC -0.25%)23.7 P/E ratio. The stock is still a buy, but after a 40% run-up this year, the upside may be more limited. Luckily, that doesn't affect its dividend.

Coca-Cola is always a good long-term investment, but with bear-market fears lingering, a short-term silver lining is that the stock typically outperforms the market during sell-offs. Past results don't guarantee future performance, but Coca-Cola has strong momentum at a time when the tech sector is dragging down the broader market.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that smaller firms are hit hardest.
  • “Suddenly, I’ll hear a string of bad language and ask what’s going on,” Blackmagic Design chief executive Grant Petty told the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electronics makers have set up procurement “war rooms” to hunt for memory chips. Prices for some chips have risen tenfold in a year, Jiyoung Sohn and Sooyoung Rhee reported for The Wall Street Journal. Staff scour eBay, call hundreds of brokers and buy batches as small as five to 12 units, the newspaper found.

Sources indicate that smaller firms are hit hardest. Large buyers can lock in supply through long-term deals with the chipmakers. Others rely on brokers and the grey market. Some sellers there mix used chips into orders of upcoming ones, the Journal reported.

“Suddenly, I’ll hear a string of bad language and ask what’s going on,” Blackmagic Design chief executive Grant Petty told the Journal.

Taiwanese memory module maker Apacer has taken out loans so it has cash ready whenever supply appears, according to the report.

In a recent development, “If chips show up, we take it. This is crazy, but there is no other way,” Apacer president Gibson Chen told the Journal.

Thieves took about $100,000 of flash memory from one manufacturer’s warehouse in Indonesia, the paper reported. The firm suspects a former employee.

It has been revealed that the Journal also carried a second-hand account of a meeting between Elon Musk and Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong. Capital Group’s Carl Kawaja stated Musk told him about it in June. Musk asked for a long-term memory deal, and Lee replied that everyone offers that.

“We get that offer from everyone. What else can you do for us?” Lee asked, according to Kawaja’s account.

Recent findings suggest that musk then offered to guarantee financing for a newly introduced Samsung chip plant, Kawaja mentioned, and got the same answer. TNW has not independently verified the account. Sam Altman has also courted the manufacturer, meeting Samsung’s presidents in October.

Industry observers note that the shortage comes as Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron move production to the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips. SK Hynix has noted tight supply could last until 2030.

Consumers are already paying. In India, around 48 Samsung and Xiaomi phone models went up by ₹1,000 to ₹4,000 in mid-November, Inc42 reported. Samsung’s Galaxy A07 5G now costs ₹22,999, up from ₹20,999.

Recent findings suggest that AI start-ups are feeling it in the cloud. GPU rental prices in India have risen 30% to 35% since February, Subhashish Banerjee, co-founder of Bharat1 AI, told Inc42. Providers now want three to six month commitments from start-ups that once booked a few hours at a time.

Recent findings suggest that some are cutting their needs instead. SquadStack, which runs voice AI agents, built smaller models trained on its own call data. Fewer tokens per call cut its costs even as hardware got pricier, chief executive Apurv Agrawal told Inc42. Memory costs have also hit Xiaomi’s quarterly profit and Apple’s margins.

By David Dierking – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:03AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

In a recent development, anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just completed the largest IPO in history, raising around $93.5 billion at $83 per share. The stock closed Nov. 20 at $88.91.

In a recent development, given that it's now one of the largest publicly traded companies in the world, you might assume its addition to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) is imminent. It isn't, actually, and won't be for a while. But the stock will show up in several other major indexes within days.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Recent findings suggest that when Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) debuted earlier this year, there was a lot of discussion around how the major indexes would handle it. Typically, companies go public at much smaller market caps, not with market caps over $1 trillion. Index committees needed to decide whether to "fast track" these mega IPOs into the indexes sooner, given their outsize influence.

Sources indicate that several providers made changes. But Standard & Poor's did not. It elected to keep the existing 12-month waiting period and generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) income requirements -- companies need to be profitable in the most recent quarter as well as the sum of the past four quarters in order to qualify.

Anthropic, so far, falls far short on the GAAP income requirement, reporting a net loss of roughly $104 billion in the first nine months of this year.

Given these requirements, the earliest we're likely to see Anthropic in the S&P 500 is late 2027.

The S&P 500 will actually be the exception, not the rule, when it comes to adding Anthropic.

The Nasdaq-100 index updated its inclusion criteria as a result of the SpaceX IPO. Now, if a company's entire market capitalization ranks within the top 40 current constituents in the index, it can be added to the index after just 15 trading days. Since Anthropic is listed on the Nasdaq, it could show up in the Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ -0.65%) before the end of the year.

The Morningstar indexes, which acquired the widely-used CRSP indexes, could add Anthropic after the close of the fifth trading day. The Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -0.18%) would be one of the biggest funds impacted by this. FTSE Russell works on a similar timeline.

Sources indicate that A lot of index funds will weight stocks according to the number of publicly available shares, not necessarily the total market cap. Since only about 5% of Anthropic's total market cap is now traded publicly, its starting weight will likely be small. Vanguard has projected only a 0.055% to 0.15% weighting for Anthropic in the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF.

When and if additional shares become publicly available, the anticipated weighting of these stocks would likely grow along with it.

If you really want to own Anthropic, you should probably just buy Anthropic.

It has been revealed that the stock won't show up at all in the S&P 500 for the foreseeable future. For many of the major large-cap indexes and corresponding ETFs, the initial weight probably won't get much above 0.25%. The exception might be the Nasdaq-100, the Invesco QQQ ETF, and the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM -0.66%). They could see an allocation closer to 1% given the more concentrated nature of that index.

It'll likely be a similar story to what we saw when SpaceX went public: a lot of hype but minimal impact to the ETF marketplace and your portfolio in general.

In a recent development, long-term investors almost certainly shouldn't be making significant asset allocation changes based on this. Even if you want to overweight tech based on a belief that Anthropic might spark the sector, your tech ETFs aren't going to meaningfully change in the future.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring latest challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also reveals how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

Richard Teng, then Binance’s head of regional markets, at Binance Blockchain Week 2023 in Istanbul.

Binance has lifted the last of the withdrawal limits it put in place after its record $6.3 billion hack in October. The exchange noted on Thursday that its withdrawal recovery work is complete.

“Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the October security incident has been fully lifted,” Binance mentioned.

Sources indicate that A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance or planned upgrades. Binance stated those pauses cover a very small share of normal traffic and are separate from the recovery.

Binance halted withdrawals after the breach on 29 October and began restoring them on 1 November, starting with Bitcoin. Deposits stayed open throughout, crypto.news reported.

Industry observers note that the first day brought a rush. Customers took out $4.65 billion and put in $1.01 billion in the first nine and a half hours on 1 November, the exchange mentioned. That left a net outflow of $3.64 billion. Binance reopened 87 more networks in the week to 14 November.

In a recent development, the exchange has said it covered the stolen assets with more than $6.34 billion of its own money. It drew on its corporate treasury, part of its user protection fund and part of its futures insurance fund. It has pledged to rebuild the user fund to about $1 billion, and published a reserve snapshot covering 198 tokens.

Wallets linked to the hack moved another $35.52 million in Ether on Thursday, according to blockchain tracker Onchain Lens. It put the hackers’ remaining unfrozen holdings at about $1.9 billion.

US authorities and private companies have frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen crypto. The Justice Department also won court approval to seize more than $1.2 billion of it, The Block reported on 12 November.

In a recent development, the FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the theft. Binance stated a fake job interview gave the attackers their way in. Days after the hack, the exchange insisted it was in ‘very strong’ health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re an artist and you use social media, you’ve probably heard about Ohuhu by now. This brand swiftly made a name for itself simply because they offered high-quality alcohol based markers at prices that undercut competitors. I have to admit that I turned my nose up at them at first; I didn’t believe they could be as good as the markers I already owned when they cost so much less.

Recent findings suggest that in short, I should have listened to Ohuhu’s supporters. I was able to try out both the Honolulu 2S alcohol markers, and my first ever set of acrylics with the Hilo brush tip acrylic paint markers. I was blown away by both.

In a recent development, perfect for artists of all skill levels, the Ohuhu Hilo markers come in packs of 48 or 72 and are an affordable option compared to rivals. They have a soft brush tip and can be layered up on the page for an opaque finish.

Recent findings suggest that ohuhu's Honolulu 2S alcohol markers come in a huge range of colors, with 320 markers in the biggest set! These dual-ended markers feature a brush and a chisel tip. While you'll need to watch out for bleed through, they produce a beautiful and smooth finish.

I started off with the Hilo acrylic markers. These markers have a single, soft and flexible brush tip, and you can currently get either a set of 48 or a set of 72 at Amazon. I was excited to see how they would perform, so I stuck a Holiday movie on, sat back and got out a coloring book to test them out.

As soon as the pen touched the page, I was immediately struck by the vibrancy of the colors and the opacity of the ink. Sure, the first sections of color I filled in were the blacks, but I couldn’t believe my eyes when the numbers almost disappeared under the acrylic ink. Some of the colors are less effective at this than others — but layer the ink up a few times, and you’ll have one gorgeously clean looking coloring page!

It has been revealed that as for the experience of using them, the soft tips give plenty of control. They felt incredibly smooth to use across gentle curves and coloring medium to large areas was easy and comfortable. These acrylic markers give you the ability to go over and redo areas you’re not happy with if you accidentally color over something you didn’t want to, which is a huge bonus.

Industry observers note that another positive under this set’s belt is the carrying case.The design is so cheerful that it immediately put a smile on my face the first time I saw it, and it honestly still does every time I open it. And compared to other name brand acrylic markers, they’re significantly cheaper — the 72 set works out to around 70 cents per marker at the Black Friday sale price.

There are some downsides to contend with. When it came to coloring small, detailed areas... I pretty much had to forget about staying within the lines. I struggled to achieve fine pointed shapes and found that the ink pooled into circular shapes every time I attempted them. I also had challenges with streaky ink, and my coloring paper pilled in certain spots, too.

This is my first time using acrylic markers, so I’m willing to acknowledge all these problems could come down to my lack of skills. I’m going to keep using them and see if I can improve my technique and layer up more to combat the streaks. The pilling probably isn’t going away until I get a coloring book with higher quality paper, though.

In a recent development, next up, I tried the Honolulu 2S alcohol based markers. You get more color options here as the sets come in packs of 24 all the way up to 320; and these markers have a dual tip. One side has a brush tip, and the other is a chisel tip.

Recent findings suggest that compared to the Hilo's, the Honolulu 2S’s brush tip is firmer and stiffer. Even though the Hilo brush tip felt great, I liked the Honolulu 2S’s firmer brush tip even more, and found it easier to control when coloring detailed areas and sharp points. It still handles curves just as well, and the chisel tip comes in handy for filling large areas too. I fell in love with alcohol-based markers years back because they produce a beautiful, non-streaky finish. The Honolulu 2S markers absolutely live up to that and looked fantastic on the page.

However, using alcohol based inks comes with more of a learning curve. I started off filling in a large black area on the page once again, and was very impressed that the marker didn’t bleed much at all. However, other colors like the dark blue and gray didn’t fare so well, and bled right over the lines.

It has been revealed that the bleed can be mitigated by using paper made specifically for alcohol markers, but you don’t have that option if you want to color in a specific coloring book. It took an hour or two for me to get used to it, but I eventually learned to leave plenty of space while filling areas in to account for the bleed.

As well as bleeding over the lines, I also had to watch out for the ink bleeding through the paper — Ohuhu provides a plastic sheet to place under your work to avoid staining the next page in your sketchbook. The ink in the Honolulu 2S markers was clearly visible on the back side of the paper I colored on (seen on the left of the image below,) but none got through to the next page. Meanwhile, the back side of the page I colored with the Hilo markers (seen on the right below) was completely clean.

If you’re a budding artist, I highly recommend picking up a set of Ohuhu markers. The Hilo acrylic markers are the ones for you if you want the most vibrancy, and are also great if you want to have the option to redo areas if you’re not happy with them. Meanwhile, the Honolulu 2S markers stand out for their enormous color selection, excellent brush tip and super-smooth finish.

These markers are cheaper than the major brands, and are even better value when discounted. Grab them while you can!

Latest Update: Scott Aaronson says AI labs are sitting on cryptography ‘bombshells’

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (455 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Computer scientist Scott Aaronson states he is “virtually certain” that leading AI labs are holding back results that would break some of today’s cryptography.
  • “Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area,” Aaronson wrote.
  • Until he sees details or hears from someone at a lab, he feels “much, much less confident” about what exactly they are.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Computer scientist Scott Aaronson states he is “virtually certain” that leading AI labs are holding back results that would break some of today’s cryptography. He made the claim in a post on his blog, Shtetl-Optimized, on Wednesday. He also warned that he does not know what those results actually are.

“Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area,” Aaronson wrote.

Until he sees details or hears from someone at a lab, he feels “much, much less confident” about what exactly they are. TNW has not independently verified the claims.

Recent findings suggest that the post followed a comment Aaronson left on his blog on Tuesday. In it, he said he had heard “many, many rumors” that one or both labs had a fast way to factor large numbers. That would break RSA, the encryption behind much of the web’s security. The comment spread widely on X, and he later added a note to it.

“A rumor is a rumor is a rumor, and the parts that I’m ‘virtually certain’ about fall well short of Factoring in P,” he wrote.

Google published a paper on Wednesday with a new factoring algorithm. Aaronson remarked it held big theoretical results, but nothing of practical use for breaking encryption.

The rumours come during a run of maths results from OpenAI and Anthropic. On Tuesday, both labs published proofs of VP ≠ VNP. The problem has long been seen as a step towards P ≠ NP, the most famous open question in computer science.

OpenAI also posted a paper claiming that the exponent of matrix multiplication is exactly 9/4. The 111-page paper states multiplying two n×n matrices takes at least n9/4/2 multiplication or division steps. The question dates back to Volker Strassen’s work in the late 1960s.

Last week, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge mentioned he and Claude had proved the Riemann hypothesis. The Lean proof assistant has since certified the proof. In October, OpenAI said its model had disproved a famous hypothesis.

“I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far,” Aaronson wrote.

It has been revealed that he asked readers not to let cryptography overshadow the maths. If their main worry was a Bitcoin wallet, he wrote, they should look for rumours elsewhere. He also urged people to accept that the AI proofs are real, now that labs back them with Lean certificates.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research indicates the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”.

Recent findings suggest that per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the organization from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:.

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”.

#131286. Is Micron Stock a Buy After HPE Stated Memory Will Stay Scarce Into 2028?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (861 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

Is Micron Stock a Buy After HPE Stated Memory Will Stay Scarce Into 2028?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +1.57%) told investors on Nov.
  • "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least the second half of calendar 2028," CEO Antonio Neri said on the firm's earnings call that evening.
  • In a recent development, that seems like good news for Micron Technology (MU -4.53%), which makes DRAM (the memory computers use while they work) and NAND flash storage chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:17AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +1.57%) told investors on Nov. 23 that it still can't get all the memory chips it wants. And it doesn't think that'll change soon.

"We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least the second half of calendar 2028," CEO Antonio Neri said on the firm's earnings call that evening.

In a recent development, that seems like good news for Micron Technology (MU -4.53%), which makes DRAM (the memory computers use while they work) and NAND flash storage chips. But the memory maker's shares slid anyway. Micron closed at $707.70 on Nov. 23, just before the call. As of this writing on Nov. 25, the stock traded near $550, less than half the $1,213.56 it closed at on June 25, its record.

Meanwhile, BNP Paribas downgraded the shares, saying memory supply might catch up to demand a year sooner than it had thought.

The tech firm noted in March that DRAM and NAND make up over half the cost of the parts in a traditional server. And its inventory more than doubled in fiscal 2026, from around $6.4 billion on Oct. 31, 2025, to $11.8 billion by July 31 and $14.1 billion by Oct. 31, 2026.

Industry observers note that HPE's timeline seems to have stretched, too. In March, Neri said he expected high DRAM and NAND prices to "persist well into 2027.".

In a recent development, CFO Marie Myers remarked the $14.1 billion inventory reflected higher costs for commodity parts like memory, purchases for customer orders, and what she called "strategic buys." She added that HPE's commodity costs climbed by significant double-digit percentages in 2026, and she expects smaller increases ahead. But smaller increases are still increases, not the price drops a glut would cause.

BNP Paribas thinks one could. In a note reported on Nov. 24, it cut its rating on Micron to neutral from outperform. It now notes DRAM and NAND supply and demand might approach balance starting in mid-2027 and drive average selling prices down. It flagged risks to big cloud companies' data center plans for 2028 and newly introduced factory capacity coming online.

Recent findings suggest that micron's stock dropped 11% that day, and again on Nov. 25, when research firm TrendForce stated NAND flash might move into oversupply in 2027. TrendForce still expects DRAM to stay tight through 2027, and DRAM made up about three-quarters of Micron's revenue in fiscal 2026.

According to recent reports, part of the newly introduced factory capacity BNP mentioned is Micron's own. Its first new fab in Idaho should start making wafers in mid-2027, and a facility in Taiwan should begin meaningful shipments around then too. But Micron notes output at a new fab ramps up over a few quarters. And its other planned fabs, including a second one in Idaho and a new NAND factory in Singapore, aren't set to start output until the second half of 2028 or later.

According to recent reports, "[W]e do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance," management wrote about DRAM in Micron's prepared remarks for its Sept. 30 earnings call.

Industry observers note that HPE's 2028 date matches Micron's building schedule. BNP's earlier date seems to rely more on demand weakening.

Recent findings suggest that micron's fiscal 2028 ends on Aug. 31, 2028, so HPE's outlook covers nearly all of the year. If the outlook holds, Micron could spend most of fiscal 2028 selling into a market still short on chips. If BNP is right, prices could be dropping for most of it.

The stock price looks closer to the second case.

At roughly $550, Micron trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 7.4 on its fiscal 2026 results. Based on the average analyst estimate for fiscal 2028, the price is below 3 times earnings.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Sources indicate that even BNP sees Micron's earnings per share bottoming at $86 in 2029, over the $74.33 per share Micron earned in fiscal 2026 under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). The stock looks cheap even on that bearish estimate.

One buyer's view could be wrong, of course. But I think HPE's outlook undercuts the glut worries, especially for DRAM, Micron's largest business. A buyer still stocking up at higher prices is tough to square with a stock priced for falling memory prices by mid-2027.

I'd consider buying some Micron shares here, in a position small enough to ride out more days like Nov. 24. If HPE starts pulling that 2028 date forward, like BNP just did with its own, I'd rethink that.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that canada is adding C$700M to its AI Compute Access Fund, taking it to C$1B, with bigger subsidies for companies that use Canadian-owned computing.
  • Industry observers note that canada is adding C$700M to a fund that helps smaller companies pay for the computing power behind AI, the government said on Thursday.
  • It has been revealed that the fund helps pay for the cloud computing firms need to build and run AI products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that canada is adding C$700M to its AI Compute Access Fund, taking it to C$1B, with bigger subsidies for companies that use Canadian-owned computing. A first new call targets health and life sciences, and 45 more firms are getting C$52M from the fund’s first phase.

Industry observers note that canada is adding C$700M to a fund that helps smaller companies pay for the computing power behind AI, the government said on Thursday. That takes the AI Compute Access Fund to C$1B, up from C$300M.

It has been revealed that the fund helps pay for the cloud computing firms need to build and run AI products. In its new phase, it pays more when they use computing that is owned and run in Canada. The aim is to create demand for local providers.

“Canadian ideas need Canadian computing power,” said Evan Solomon, Canada’s minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation.

It has been revealed that the first upcoming funding round is open to health and life sciences projects. Solomon also revealed more than C$52M for 45 companies from the fund’s first phase, bringing its total to over C$118M for 89 firms. Last month, Ottawa also put C$2.5M into helping 25 Prairie firms adopt AI.

Recent findings suggest that the money comes from Canada’s national AI strategy, unveiled in June. Ottawa has also pledged to bring 500 megawatts of its own AI computing online.

In October, it backed Cohere’s C$7bn funding round. Foreign firms are interested too: OpenAI has remarked Canada has the energy and land for data centres.
